When you, who gather the fruit of these words,
Feed here like the reaper and sower of the ploughman,
So that you may remember the diligence and work of the scribe,
I ask you, consider his name and repay him in turn.
The origin of these little verses, answering to those who ask,
Declares it to the seeker and gives knowledge to the willing.
Consider what kind of letters are capital,
From which a name will quickly appear as a sign,
Just as you see at the bottom of the first verse.

This book is finished in the year of our Lord 1519 on the Sunday after the day of Saint Peter and Paul, the holy apostles, to honor God and His beloved mother and the most holy mother, Saint Anne. And all those who shall use this book should remember the writer with a Our Father and Hail Mary to honor the holy mother Saint Anne so that they may obtain her grace and mercy in this time and after this time, eternal joy. Amen. Her name is Sister Gretgen Smytz.

[Apparamment il faut comprendre que Sustef a préparé le livre pour Fye. Au f.9v°, elle donnait les obits de son père, d'un frère et d'une sœur (1467-1477); plus tard (?) elle (?) ajoutait ceux de l'oncle Ansse (1468; sans doute le père de Fye), de deux autres frères (1468, 1481) et les noms d'une sœur et de Suster elle-même (ces deux étant encore en vie). details.value: Presens opus cum alijs XII voluminibus incepit fr. Franciscus Mathie de observantia O.Min. sub vicario provinciali patre utique rev. Iohanne de Lindefelcz apud s. Claram in Bamberga in cenobio seu domuncula confessoris virginum atque sororum s. Clare sub abbatissa Katharina Sensenschmidin Iudoco Cutzenbach confessore bene digno cuius anima requiescat in pace. a. incarn. ... 1498 circa festum assumptionis Marie v. et feliciter determinavit manu propria prememoratus fr. Franciscus presbiterorum minimus in litera non (!) illuminatione reliigatione atque correctione sub rev. p. Iohanne Keller proviciali vicario generosa abbatissa Dorothea Marchionissa patre Frederico Gerberstorfer confessore pro tunc existente utique famoso a. salutis 1501 in vig. festi purificationis Marie immaculate virg. (etc.)

This present work, along with twelve other volumes, was begun by Brother Franciscus Mathie of the Observant branch of the Friars Minor, under the provincial vicar, the reverend Father Johannes of Lindefelcz, at St. Clare’s in Bamberg, in the small monastery or residence of the confessor of the virgins and sisters of St. Clare, under Abbess Katharina Sensenschmid, with the worthy confessor Jodocus Cutzenbach, whose soul may rest in peace. In the year of the Incarnation 1498, around the feast of the Assumption of the Virgin Mary, it was happily completed by the same Brother Franciscus, the least of priests, with his own hand. The work was not (!) illuminated, bound, or corrected under the reverend Father Johannes Keller, provincial vicar, the noble Abbess Dorothea Marchioness, and Father Frederico Gerberstorfer, the well-known confessor at that time, in the year of salvation 1501, on the eve of the feast of the Purification of the Immaculate Virgin Mary (etc.).
Bamberg, fr. Franciscus presbiterorum, fr. (s) and Dorothea Marchionissa (proof) at time of Katharina Sensenschmidin)

Large initials, up to approximately 23 cm high and wide, with foliate ornament extending over a large part of the margin, executed very carefully in gold and various colors; eight include figurative representations, see above. In addition there are four purely ornamental initials:
	•	fol. 14v: S
	•	fol. 44: U at Transfiguratio
	•	fol. 70: M at nat. apostolorum
	•	fol. 141: T at In anniversario ecclesiae

Elsewhere there are large initials sketched in red and blue or black, the latter often with human faces. The margins have often been mutilated by heavy trimming.

One Ave Maria, for God’s sake, for the scribe, as it was often difficult for her. This book is completed in the year of our Lord, when one wrote 1526, on St. Ambrose’s Day in Lent at eight in the morning, and may God be eternally praised for it. Sister Lijsbeth Witjens and Sister Magriet Raes have written in this book. After over eighteen years of writing, Sister Kathlinen van Molenbeke completed and ended it on the eve of Our Lady's Day of the 15th taps, on the eve of Saint Cecilia, in the year of our Lord 1489. At that time, she was approximately 51 years old. Please, from your heart, recite an Ave Maria for the three of them, so that God may grant them glory for their labor in eternity.
This book belongs to the cloister of the Roses Planted in Jericho within Brussels, near Saint Kathlinen.

This book was written in the year of our Lord 1510 by Sister Johanna Colijns when she was fifty-six years old. And she donated it to the convent out of goodwill from Jericho on the eighth day of July, when her income fell on the Jubilee Year of the year 1511. Praying for her poor soul to be faithful so that she may live with Christ in the end. Amen. This book contains thirty-one quaternions and it took five reams of paper and five leaves.

details.value: INt Jaer ons heren M cccc lxxii tich. Op sinte peeters ende pauwels dach in junio. Begonste suster katherina van ghiseghem profes nonne in onsen cloester te iericho aen dit boec vanden tabernakel te scriuen. Ende sij volyndet int selue iaer iiii dage in april op sinte ambrosius dach. die viel opten sondach. Dit heeftse ter eren gods ende om gemeyn stichtinge met groeter nersticheit bearbeit in allen wtgesochten tijden als sij int gemeyn werck niet sijn en moeste. doense was out xxvi tich iaer. Bidt om die minne gods voer haer ewige salicheit. Dit boec behoert toe. den cloestere van onser lieuer vrouwen rose geplant in iericho. bynnen bruesele bi sinte katherinen. der ordenen sinte augustijns. soe wie dat vint geeft den relygiosen ioffrouwen weder om gods wille.

In the year of our Lord one thousand four hundred seventy-two. On the feast day of Saints Peter and Paul in June, Sister Katherina van Ghiseghem, professed nun in our cloister at Jericho, began to write this book on the tabernacle. And she completed it in the same year, on the fourth day of April, on the feast day of Saint Ambrose, which fell on a Sunday. She did this in honor of God and for the common edification with great diligence, working on it diligently at all chosen times when she was not engaged in communal work. She was twenty-six years old at the time. Pray for her eternal salvation out of love for God. This book belongs to the cloister of Our Lady Rose-planted in Jericho, within Brussels, near Saint Catherine's, of the Augustinian order. Whoever finds it, return it to the religious ladies for the love of God.

details.value: Hier beghint die prologe op die navolghende sermoenen die welke onse eerwerdige pater her jan storm hevet ghepredict in onsen cloestere te jhericho: doen hi ons commissarijs ende rector tsamen was. welke sermoenen onse werdige mater. doen sij noch inden staet der prelaturen niet en was. aensiende den swaren last ende arbeit des selven Eerbaren vaders crech minne ende devocie dese sermoenen te bescriven: op dat den arbeit des predicaers inder ewiger glorien met nyewen loene vergouden worde soe dicke als yemens devocie beweeght wert. uut aenhoerne oft selve te studeerne dese sermoene. Laet ons ghetrouwelijc bidden voer onsen eerwerdigen pater die den arbeit heeft ghedaen inder predicatien. ende voer onser ghemijnder mater: suster marie van pee god wil haer geven sinen ewegen vree die den arbeit heeft ghedaen om dit te bescriven ... soe hebic dit navolgende boec ghepijnt te vergaderen uut veel collacien die in onsen godshuyse gepredict sijn binnen vijf jaren ..."

Hier ynden die sermoenen ons Eerweerdeghen paters welke ic van velen een weynich vergadert hebbe tot mijns selfs orbore ende der gheendere dier in believen sal te studeren Ende sij waren volscreven int jaer ons heren. M. iii[c]. ende lxvi. op sinte laureis des gloriosen maerteleers dach voer vesperen
Dit boeck was volscreven Int jaer ons heren doemen screef.Dusent. vierhondert. seven ende tsestich. des sesten daeghs in septembri. op enen sondach

Here begins the prologue to the following sermons, which our venerable father, Master Jan Storm, preached in our convent at Jericho, when he was both our commissary and rector. These sermons our worthy mother—while she was not yet in the office of prioress—out of compassion for the great burden and labor of that honorable father, was moved by love and devotion to have them written down, so that the labor of the preacher might be rewarded in eternal glory with renewed grace each time someone’s devotion is stirred to hear or to study these sermons. Let us therefore devoutly pray for our venerable father, who performed the labor of preaching, and for our worthy mother, Sister Marie van Pee—may God grant her His eternal peace—who undertook the labor of writing this down. … Thus I have taken pains to gather this following book from many sermons that were preached in our house of God over the course of five years.

Here end the sermons of our Venerable fathers, which I have gathered a few of for my own edification and for those who wish to study. And they were completed in the year of our Lord, 1366, on the feast of Saint Laurence, the glorious martyr, before vespers.
This book was completed in the year of our Lord when it was written. Fourteen hundred and sixty-seven, on the sixth day of September, on a Sunday.

(This is not the Dorothea von Kippenheim OP mentioned in VL 2 [1980], col. 218; rather, it refers to another sister of the same name who lived in the Unterlinden convent in the early 16th century [VL 11 (2004), col. 380].)

According to Hamburger (2000–2001) the decorative style does not necessarily point to the origin of the book decoration in the Unterlinden monastery, but rather to an external workshop, although possibly located in Colmar itself and committed to a common »style alsacien des années 1500«.

f. 145v: Explicit apparatus super arbore consanguinitatis et affinitatis compitus a domino Iohanne Andrea decreerum doctore et scriptus per me sororem Lauream de Bossis

Heavily decorated, miniatures, historiated initials.
The decoration consists of two large miniatures with a frontispiece on folios 4v and 5r, thus facing each other. The miniature on folio 4v (129 x 200 mm) depicts the Annunciation. Below the miniature is the evangelical inscription: ne timeas Maria invenisti gratiam, while above appears the monogram IHS; the miniature on folio 5r (133 x 205 mm) depicts the offering of the book by the author Giovanni d'Andrea to Pope Boniface VIII. Within the text, there are 6 rubricated initials, 413 filigree initials, 74 decorated illuminated initials, and 1 figurative initial, along with one decorated initial, and two figurative initials in the prologues on folios 4v-5r. In the gloss, there are 373 filigree initials and 77 illuminated initials. In the Apparatus, however, there are two filigree initials and one decorated illuminated initial. The manuscript's decoration is attributed to the copyist Laura Bossi, with the exception of the miniatures, which Giuseppa Zanichelli attributes to a Pavia artist from the last quarter of the 15th century who collaborated with the "master of the yellow backgrounds." Zanichelli attributes the name "Master of Laura Bossi" to this artist.

details.value:
Produced, signed, and dated by the Spanish nun Maria Dies de Oña, this early sixteenth-century Spanish manuscript gradual contains the “propers” and choral chants for the Mass for Cistercian Use, according to the pre-Tridentine liturgical calendar. Although a complete volume, it is not a complete work as it contains approximately only the first third of the liturgical year, from the first Sunday in Advent to Palm Sunday. Given the size and format of this volume, the complete gradual for the entire liturgical year would have been represented by three or four volumes.

Produced by a female religious copyist for use by the female monastery of San Salvador de Oña in Burgos, this substantial volume is almost entirely composed of chant and does not include the long spoken portions of the Mass. Minor leaf repairs, occasional corrections, marginal additions, and instructions for following the text indicate that this manuscript was used on a regular basis.

details.value: Do man zalt von der geburt unsere heren Christi 1483 an s. Silvestertag han ich Dorothe von Hof dis buoch ungeschriben und bin davor ze herbst an s. Frenentag im 1482 iar alt gesin 24 iar und ist gesin nün iar an s; Pallus bekert im 83 iar, das Jerg und ich elich zesamen kamen. Liebe überwint alle alle ding. Deo gratias. Item und do ich alt bin gesin 19 iar uf s. Verenatag, do gieng ich uf des hl. crütztag nächst darnach genden Einsideln uf ain engelwiche und Satz do den sturtz uf und let etliche weltliche claider und clainet hin, das ich yr nit me truog.

In the year of our Lord’s birth 1483, on St. Sylvester’s Day, I, Dorothea von Hof, wrote out this book. And in the previous autumn, on St. Fridolin’s Day in the year 1482, I was 24 years old. And it was nine years since St. Paul’s Conversion Day in the year ’83 that Jörg and I were joined together in marriage. Love overcomes all things. Deo gratias.

357r [Lang]): Do man zalt von der geburt unsere heren Christi 1483 an s. Silvestertag han ich Dorothe von Hof dis buoch ungeschriben und bin davor ze herbst an s. Frenentag im 1482 iar alt gesin 24 iar und ist gesin nün iar an s; Pallus bekert im 83 iar, das Jerg und ich elich zesamen kamen. Liebe überwint alle alle ding. Deo gratias. Item und do ich alt bin gesin 19 iar uf s. Verenatag, do gieng ich uf des hl. crütztag nächst darnach genden Einsideln uf ain engelwiche und Satz do den sturtz uf und let etliche weltliche claider und clainet hin, das ich yr nit me truog.

Written by Dorothea von Hof at the age of 25
scribe, Dorothea von Hof, née Ehingerin
Dorothea von Hof (1458-1501)
From the possession of Margarete Ehingerin, née Neidhart (died 1513), married since 1482 to the Constance patrician Hans Ehinger (1456–1505), son of Heinrich Ehinger and Margarete von Kappel; cf.the alliance coat of arms Ehinger/Neidhart 2r and the ownership entry 357r: This book belongs to Margreth Ehingerjn in Mergstat. Contrary to earlier opinions, it was therefore not the older Margarete Ehinger, née von Kappel (died 1490?), but rather her daughter-in-law who owned this manuscript (cf.Gebauer [2010] p. 37 f.[with family tree]); she was thus likely also the sister-in-law of the scribe, Dorothea von Hof, née Ehingerin. Regarding three other manuscripts from the possession of the older Ehinger generation, see Nos. 36.0.2. (Einsiedeln Stiftsbibliothek, Codex 710), No. 43.1.55. (Einsiedeln, Stiftsbibliothek, Codex 283), and No. 59.2.5. (St. Gallen, Kantonsbibliothek, VadSlg. Ms. 343 c–d).

In the name of Lord (Jesus) (Christ) [then 'ella' crossed out] and of the glorious Virgin Mary, mother of God, and of Lord Saint John the Baptist, on the day of whose conception this book was begun, the 24th day of September 1488.

This book belongs to the nuns of the Paradiso, copied by me Sister Raffaella with much effort and hardship. And it is the eighth that I have copied, all for the spiritual consolation of my sisters in (Christ), and I do not believe I will copy more except for the Corona of the monks, which I have started in another volume. And if the letter is rustic, the author and the words are worthy, and therefore it should be regarded.
Amen. Finished on the 23rd day of June 1496

Suor Angela has been identified as Angela de’Rucellai, Dominican nun of San Jacopo di Ripoli (Levi D’Ancona, Miniatura e miniatori, 11) or as another copist from the same monastery, suor Angela Miniberti or Angela Mineberti (Pini Gruppo di codici, 267-268) Latham states: “This manuscript, also called the Manuale, contained all the prayers, the antiphonals, and the hymns, used by the nuns in their religious services.
Bradley I 38: a nun of the monastery of St. James or Ripoli. Her family name was Miniberti

details.value: Finissi di scrivere il detto libro negli anni del Signore mille quattrocento novanta Quattro, addì X d’aghosto. Iscritto con gran faticha e disagio la maggior parte di nocte al lume di lucerna. Prieghovi non ghuardiate alla rusticità della lettera, ma pigliate la sana e verace doctrina data dalla bocca della verità e della sua gloriosa madre virgho Maria alla nostra madre sancta Brigida. Priegho che chi llo leggie con diligentia lo tengha e cchi ll’acatta sì lo renda
Questo libro è delle suore e monache del Paradiso. Suor Cleofe.

I finished writing the said book in the year of the Lord one thousand four hundred ninety-four, on the 10th of August. Written with great effort and hardship, mostly at night by lamplight. I ask you not to judge the simplicity of the letter, but to take the sound and true doctrine given by the mouth of the Truth and his glorious mother, the Virgin Mary, to our holy mother, Saint Bridget. I pray that whoever reads it diligently may keep it, and whoever buys it may return it.
This book belongs to the sisters and nuns of the Paradiso. Sister Cleofe.

details.value: Al nome di Dio, a dì 4 d'aprile 1484. Questo o ritrato a mia chonsolatione delle prediche di maestro Mariano romano, di quaresima, in Santa Maria del Fiore in Firenze. Se ci fusi manchamento, sarebe mio difetto: non arei tenuto bene a mente. Io Margherita figliuola di meser Tommaso Soderini o scritto questo di mia mano. Chi lo legie prieghi Idio per me. Se gli è scritto bene, è stato dono di Dio e Lui ringratio. Tutto el bene vien da Dio, tutto el male son io
Di maestro Mariano. Al nome di Dio, a dì 4 di marzo 1488 [1489 in stile comune]. S'io dicho bene, è dono di Dio, s'io dicho [le ultime due parole riscritte] male, son io che o pocha memoria.

In the name of God, on the 4th day of April 1484. This I have copied for my consolation from the sermons of Master Mariano the Roman, preached during Lent in Santa Maria del Fiore in Florence. If there are errors, it would be my fault: I did not keep them well in memory. I, Margherita, daughter of Messer Tommaso Soderini, wrote this with my own hand. Whoever reads it, pray to God for me. If it is written well, it was a gift of God, and I thank Him. All good comes from God; all evil is from me.
Of Master Mariano. In the name of God, on the 4th day of March 1488 [1489 modern style]. If I speak well, it is a gift of God; if I speak badly, it is I who have little memory.

details.value: Ora deum pro me peccatrice soror Maria Horns.
Pray to God for me, a sinner, Sister Maria Horns.
27v: Ora deum pro me peccatrice soror Maria Horns

The origin in a Franciscan convent is evidenced by:
• The feast of the stigmatization of St. Francis (135r) and the rubric on f.150r referring to von unßerm werdigen vader Franciscus (“our worthy Father Francis”).
• The suffrage for Severus, unserm Patrone (“our patron”) on f.162r, situated within the liturgical year sequence between November 11 and November 21, suggesting Boppard (Archdiocese of Trier).
In 1489, Franciscan sisters from Besselich settled in Boppard, known for their manuscript production (cf.J. Marx, Geschichte des Erzstifts Trier, vol. 2, part 2, 1862, p. 423, and K. Schlegel, Besselich am Mittelrhein, 1980, p. 19).

details.value: Dit boec is ghescreven inden besloten regularersen cloester dat ghelegen is bynnen oestmal in dat mercgrefscap van hantwerpen Ende ghesticht is inder eeren der precentacien der saligher maghet ende ghebenedider moeder gods Maria Ende is gheeynt op die vigilie pasione petri et pauli der glorioser ende heiligher apostelen: van mi suster heilken jacops Een vanden vieren die dit cloester hebben helpen begynnen ter eeren gods: mer die mynste in duechden Enen Ave maria uut mynnen / Men en maech dit boec niet vercopen. want tis veel op heilighe dage ghescreven.

This book is written in the enclosed regular cloister located in Oostmalle in the county of Antwerp and established in honor of the Presentation of the Blessed Virgin Mary. details.value:
Approximately 20 hands or textual sections can be distinguished. Various forms of Bastarda script are used. Since some scripts resemble each other closely, the number of hands may in fact be smaller, and some differences may be explained by different writing phases or circumstances.

As shown by a number of scribal notes, the manuscript was written in a female convent, most likely in a Dominican nunnery. This is suggested not only by internal content-related criteria, but especially by the fact that the first demonstrable owner was probably a Dominican nun at St. Catherine’s in Nuremberg, or alternatively at Maria Medingen

On the final folio of several quires, catchwords or remnants thereof appear repeatedly (88v, 100v, 112v, 124v, 192v, 216v, 228v, 268v). It remains unclear whether catchwords were originally present throughout and were lost through trimming, or whether they were only employed by certain scribes in the sections they produced.

The manuscript is a plainly designed utilitarian volume. The texts or sections written by different hands are mostly rubricated, but to very different degrees. Often only the beginning and/or end of texts or text sections, or the transition between larger passages, are rubricated, while the remaining running text is not. Accordingly, rubrication is absent in longer sections: 44v–50r; 52r–54v; 56v–75r; 78v–83r; 84v–93r; 94r–102r; 103r–111r; 112v–116v; 117v–125v; 126v–130v; 131v–136v; 150r–153; 155–160r; 167v–170v; 257v–275v; 276r.

For the most part, rubrication therefore does not appear to have been carried out later in a single, unified process, but rather during the production of the various parts or texts of the manuscript—thus, in many cases probably by the scribes themselves.

In addition to red headings and rubricated capitals or initial letters of textual units, there are occasionally underlinings in red (especially for nomina sacra), as well as chapter and paragraph signs and corrections or deletions in red.

Simple red initials, without decorative ambition, mostly two to four lines high. At the beginning of the text on 1r, a four-line initial was planned but not executed. On 131r, there is a red D-initial, in whose interior field—appropriate to the text, a letter by Heinrich Seuse—the Christogram (Ihs) is written in red. On 233r, a red I-initial extends across most of the height of the page.

Translations of the Gospels and Acts of the Apostles

Various attempts to identify this woman as a member of a family from Bremen or a nun from a Cistercian convent in the Diocese of Erfurt could not be substantiated, especially since these attributions conflict with the Middle Rhenish writing style of the manuscript. It is clear that the later hand did not contribute to the manuscript itself, as their contribution is limited to five words, which should therefore be considered an ownership inscription.
Dating the manuscript poses challenges. Earlier research noted that the year “1404” appeared on an erasure, originally intended as “1504.” Since then, the manuscript has been dated to 1504. This late dating is further supported by watermark analysis, indicating that the earliest paper used by the scribe was not in circulation before 1480. However, the manuscript’s layout, which remains very traditional and medieval, aligns more closely with manuscripts from the early 15th century than those from around or after 1500.

At the end of Acts (f. 295r), the following scribal colophon was entered:

“Here ends the book of the Acts of the Apostles. In the year of our Lord 1504 it was written.”

A later hand added:

“by Sister Gertrut von Buren.”
Rubricated, with red Lombard initials decorated with reserved ornamentation at chapter openings and red-green fleuronné initials at the beginnings of the prologues.

On f. 7rb, a historiated E-initial in opaque colour painting, extending over thirteen lines: in front of the blue letter body, which stands on a rectangular, matte rose-violet, ornamented ground, St Catherine, turned to the left, holding a lowered sword; at her feet, the wheel. In the inner field of the initial, a flowered meadow below and punched gold leaf above. From the upper corner of the E, scrolling vines wind along the upper and outer margins.

The remaining opaque-colour initials, among them one particularly emphasised by its size (13 lines) and the elaboration of its vine ornament (f. 2rb, preface), consist of letter bodies with interlace, gem-like, or other ornament, set against an almost square framed ground decorated with floral motifs. The vines are more slender and sinuous, often elongated (frequently within the narrow intercolumnar space), rather than voluminous; as initial extensions they may be short or long and sweeping (f. 10v), or form a vine-staff supported by short initial tendrils (e.g. f. 87vb), occasionally also appearing as an independent branch beside the text column (f. 90ra). In addition, in some instances, flowers and gold pollen are executed in opaque colour painting.

details.value: The decoration appears to have been carried out in two or more phases. The original decoration most likely consisted of rubrication, versals, and colour stroking in red, plain 2-line initials in red or green, 2- and 3-line initials with interior reserved shapes in red or green, and large 7-line parted initials in blue and red. All of these were executed with a matte medium. Later, the reserved or interior spaces of most of the larger initials were coloured with red, blue, dark green and pale yellow pigment in a shiny, raised medium and pen flourishing added in lavender or red. This later decoration was done with little skill or finesse. At the same time, many of the larger initials had their interior shapes filled with circular cutouts of saints, presumably cut from prints and pasted to the page, that were also coloured.

details.value:
The text alternates between black and red ink. Red and blue Lombard initials. Many gold initials, two to thirteen lines high, some with blue and red fleuronné decoration, and a few ornamentally split.
With 133 miniatures and historiated initials, this manuscript has the richest decorative programme among the surviving Medingen manuscripts.

The decoration includes angels, saints, biblical figures, Medingen nuns, the Easter Lamb, the risen Christ, scenes from the Resurrection, Christ appearing to Mary Magdalene, Peter and John at the empty tomb, Emmaus scenes, musical angels, animals, birds, trees, and numerous scrolls with song incipits.

Several images specifically show Medingen nuns, for example on fols. 36r, 41r, 44r, 52r, 97r, 104r, 119r, 126v, and 131r.
The manuscript contains red neumes of the Metz type throughout. At the beginning they are nearly diastematic, but later they become imprecise and no longer observe pitch spacing.

records.rec_Title: Karlsruhe, Badische Landesbibliothek, Lichtent. 69; Full manuscript

details.value:
Written in a bastarda script predominantly by Sister Regula, except for:
• f.46ra (7 lines)
• f.222vb–223rb (two contemporary hands)
• f.51v (an addition around 1500).
Corrections and additions, mostly by the original scribe, are present.

Book of Holy Maidens and Women (f.1ra–223rb)
• Introduction: Discusses the four cardinal virtues symbolized by the four rivers of paradise (Ortus voluptatis).
• Legends: A collection of 57 legends of female saints, beginning with St. Mary Magdalene (Maria stabat ad monumentum foris plorans).
• Provenance: Compiled by Sister Regula, as noted in secondary literature (e.g., K. Kunze).
• Literature: The legend of Mary of Egypt has been edited by K. Kunze (1978).
2. Pseudo-Eusebius, Epistola ad Damasum de Morte Hieronymi, German Translation (f.223va–228rb, 267va–278rb)
• A medieval German adaptation of the Latin text (BHL 3866), attributed to Pseudo-Eusebius, concerning the death of St. Jerome.
• The German translation does not match other known Middle High German versions.
3. Pseudo-Jerome, Letter to His Mother on Virtues (f.229ra–240rb)
• An instructional and exhortative letter, in which “Jerome” advises his mother on virtuous living.
• The manuscript’s version is not mentioned in key reference works.
4. The Golden Pater Noster (f.240rb–243rb)
• An expanded meditation on the Pater Noster (Our Father) prayer, reflecting on its theological implications.
• Includes parallels with Patrologia Latina (PL 149, 569–576).
5. A Short Gloss on the Pater Noster (f.243rb–244ra)
• A brief guide on the meaning and spiritual significance of the prayer.
6. The School of Virtues (f.244ra–252vb)
• A didactic dialogue between a master and a novice (later referred to as a novitiate), discussing ascetic virtues and leading to eternal life.
7. Epistola ad Moniales (f.252vb–255ra)
• An exhortative letter to nuns, urging them to heed divine inspiration and embrace the love of Christ.
8. Dicta on the Gift of Tears and Prayer (f.255ra–255vb)
• Spiritual reflections and teachings attributed to Augustine, Basil, Paschasius, and Bernard.
9. An Epistle to an Abbess (f.255va–259ra)
• A letter emphasizing love and obedience, comparing divine love to the strength of death, and exalting Christ as the bridegroom of virgins.
Ascetic Instructions (f.259ra–262va)
• A text composed for the “entertainment of young cloistered nuns” by a learned priest.
• Focuses on ascetic ideals and encouragement, referring to the nuns as Christ’s chosen spouses.
• Likely written specifically for the Lichtenthal convent.
2. Another Epistle on Five Virtues (f.262va–264vb)
• Opens with Ponite corda vestra in virtute eius (Ps 47,14), emphasizing the virtues that adorn a faithful life.
• Encourages the practice of virtues to achieve eternal blessedness.
• Ends with a devotional note from the scribe, requesting a recitation of one Ave Maria.
• Mentions Liber Monasterii Lucida Vallis, linking it to Lichtenthal Abbey (often called Lucida Vallis in Latin).
3. On True Poverty (f.265ra–266ra)
• Draws on Matthew 12:1 to explore the virtue of poverty in imitation of Christ and his disciples.
• Provides a theological framework for embracing material poverty as a spiritual ideal.
4. A Consolatory Sermon by St. Bernard (f.266ra–267ra)
• Begins with Bonum est nos hic esse (Mt 17:4), using Bernard of Clairvaux’s alleged reflections to address monastic audiences.
• Discusses the joys and trials of cloistered life and the ultimate reward of eternal glory.
5. Poem on the Meaning of Suffering (f.267ra)
• A six-stanza poem offering solace to those enduring hardships, linking suffering to the promise of the Kingdom of Heaven.
• Contains irregularities in verse and stanza structure, reflecting its devotional rather than literary focus.
6. Return to Pseudo-Eusebius, Epistola ad Damasum (f.267va–278rb)
• This section resumes from f.223va, completing the translation of Pseudo-Eusebius’s text on the death of St. Jerome.

Karlsruhe, Badische Landesbibliothek, Schwarzach 19
Anna Schott (ca. 1450-after 1521), daughter of the Strasbourg mayor Peter Schott (1427-1504) and sister of the jurist, theologian, and humanist Peter Schott (1460-1490), can be traced in Strasbourg as a Dominican nun of the convents St. Agnes and St. Margaret and St. Agnes (from 1475). She was extensively educated. During the fire of the Strasbourg city library in 1870, a manuscript written by her around 1500 (.Historia sanctorum") was lost (Schlechter, Schott, p. 467). hie bi gedenken durch gott Swester Magdalena Steimerin ein unwirdige Swester Sant Clären Ordens die diß buoch geschriben hett mit einem Ave Maria (231r)

Magdalena Steimerin appears as the abbess in the annual accounts of the Strasbourg Abbey of St. Clare in 1485/86 and 1486/87 (StA Straßburg, AH 10819, 1485/86, p. 2, 1486/87, p. 1). (ff. 127v-129v) Vanden missen. 
(ff. 129v-130v) Hoe goet dattet is die misse ghehoert.

In total, seventeen manuscripts in Dutch collections are either known or suspected to have been made in Beverwijk, but most were made by the Canons Regular of St. Mary (Sion) in Beverwijk (cf. Byvanck database in Online Resources). It would be especially interesting to compare our manuscript with two Books of Hours in Dutch, one copied by brother Gherijt van Castrinchem at the convent of St. Mary in Beverwijk in 1498 (Leiden, University Library, MS B. P. L. 2747; see CMD-NL, vol. 2, no. 543 and Online Resources), and another copied in 1489, most likely at Beverwijk, and decorated with miniatures, as well as penwork flourishes that are very similar to those in our manuscript (Hague, KB, MS 79 K 5; sold by Les Enluminures in 2000). In addition, there are manuscripts which were copied elsewhere, but were acquired by the Beverwijk convent, including a Book of Hours for the use of Utrecht copied at a Charterhouse near Utrecht (Oxford, Bodleian Library, MS Douce 57).
alphanumerical leaf signatures in tiny writing in brown ink (mostly cropped),

The beautiful penwork ornamentation decorating sixty-five pages in this book include forms typical of the pen-flourishes made in North Holland at the end of the fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries. These include the “U-bends,” “eye-leaves,” pointed lines in bundles (often in violet ink in our manuscript), and the Haarlem “sunbursts”; for comparison, see contemporary manuscripts made in Haarlem and North Holland, as described by Hülsmann and Nieuwstraten, 1992. There are also wonderful pearl borders, stylized roses and aubergines; see f. 91v in our manuscript. The penwork flourishes in our manuscript are very similar to those in a Book of Hours in Dutch copied in 1498 by brother Gherijt van Castrinchem at the convent of St. Mary in Beverwijk (Leiden, University Library, MS B. P. L. 2747; see a reproduction from the Manuscrits datés conservés dans les Pays-Bas in Online Resources).

This manuscript was written in Vadstena Abbey, in the nuns scriptorium. The parchment was payed by sr Birgitta Gudmundi and it was completed at S Michaels eve 1517. It was written by one of the nuns, keeping her identity secret in the colophon on f.37v. It contained music and was intended for use in the church. There are closely related manuscripts in both Uppsala and Stockholm Libraries, either written or decorated by the same nun/nuns. The nuns had taken influence from their sisters i the Netherlands in the design of the large pen-flourished initials. One of the nuns who most frequently painted her large decorated initials in the same style as here was Christina Hansdotter Brask, but she seem to have hade successors. A very similar design can be found in KB A 12, UUB C 431, C 443, C 484, RA E 9002. Some of these are by Christina Hansdotter Brask and from the same period as this manuscript. The present mss is however executed by a much more stable hand than the Brask mss from the same period. A more suitable candidate is Katarina Gudmundsdotter, whose palaeography is in accordance with the scribe of this mss.

details.value: f.55r: Good Syster of your charyte I you pray remember the scrybeler when that ye may wit/i on aue maria or els thys swete word ihesu have marcy on my wreched syster whose name by the marcy of god rj trust"1 shall be wrytyn In the boke of lyfe Good deuote Syster I pray you to lerne thys lesson well of your master our sauyour cryst ihesu that sayth lerne of me for I am mylde and meke in hart and pray for me that I may do and haue the same

"f.55r: Good sister, in your charity, I pray you to remember the scribe when you may, with an Ave Maria or else this sweet word: 'Jhesu, have mercy on my wretched sister, whose name, by the mercy of God, I trust shall be written in the book of life.' Good devout sister, I pray you to learn this lesson well from your master, our Savior Christ Jhesu, who says, 'Learn of me, for I am mild and meek in heart,' and pray for me that I may do and have the same."

Lambeth Palace Library MS 546 is a collection of devotional material written by a number of late fifteenth- or early sixteenth-century hands. The main contents are 'The xv Sorowes of oure lady' (fos 7v-20v) and the 'golden letany' (fos 34r-51v, with a preface on fos 29r-33v),4 with devotions in English, and prayers in English and Latin making up the rest of the volume. It is with one of these devotions, specifically its colophon, that the present note is concerned.

details.value: An Antiphonal contains the choral parts sung during the celebration of the Divine Office or Mass celebrated by a monastic or other community. This type of choirbook was usually written in large format so that the whole choir could read the music at once. This example was made at the convent of St Klara in Cologne by one of the nuns, Sister Loppa de Speculo. Another surviving leaf records that Sister Jutta paid for the book while Loppa carried out the writing, lining (putting in the staves for the music), notation and illumination 'in the year 1350, when there was a great plague everywhere'. This was one of a series of books produced in the convent. The Abbess, Heylwigis von Beechoven, who had ruled the convent since 1344, is portrayed kneeling by the historiated initial of the Descent of the Holy Ghost on the Virgin and Apostles associating her prayer with this crucial event, when the Holy Spirit came to earth and the mission of the Apostles to spread the Christian revelation began. The prayer of her convent was thus part of the mission.

details.value: Hie ist volendet di legend von sand Franciscen. Die hat geschriben Elspet von Amberk in dem iar, do man zalt von Christes geburt tausent und driͦu hundert unn in dem xxxvii iar. So hat Katerina von Purchhausen geschriben di legend von sancto Antonio unn diu was in dem lxvii iar alt, da si di legend schreip. Unn di legend wurden peid geschriben unn erleuht unn vol praht nah sand Bartholomeus des naehtes tages. Swer di legend les, der pit got fur si, unn ůch fur di, di daz permeid unn daz pinten habent verrihte, daz uns got allen helfe zu den erlichen scharen des lieben herren sand Franciscen unn der werden fr owen sand Chlaren. Here is completed the legend of Saint Francis. It was written by Elspet of Amberg in the year when one counted from Christ’s birth one thousand three hundred and in the thirty-seventh year [i.e. 1337]. And Katerina of Burghausen wrote the legend of Saint Anthony, and she was sixty-seven years old when she wrote the legend. And the legends were both written and illuminated and fully completed on the day after the feast of Saint Bartholomew. Whoever reads the legends, let him pray to God for them, and also for those who carried out the parchment-making and the binding, that God may help us all to the honourable company of the beloved lord Saint Francis and the worthy lady Saint Clare. Amen.

written by Eufrosina Gärtnerin for personal use; cf. ownership entries 339v and on the inside back cover by her sister Susanna Gärtnerin:
“Item das piechlein ist gewessen S. Eiffersynna Gärtnerin in der Pitterich regelhaus, die ist verschiden am XII tag winttermonat im XVC und XXXIIII jar und ist darnach worden S. Susanna Gartneryn, got der almachtig pegnaden inen hie und dort ewiglich amen.”

(“This little book belonged to Sister Eufrosina Gärtnerin in the Pütrich-Regelhaus; she died on 12 December 1534 and it then passed to Sister Susanna Gärtnerin, may God Almighty grant them grace here and eternally there, amen.”)

Illustrations: 8 pasted-in miniatures with scenes of the Christ Child, mostly colored pen drawings:
	•	1v, parchment, 7.8 × 5.5 cm: Christ Child at a nun’s window in a convent; inscription: “Ich ste vor der tur, tue mir auf und laß mich ein du allerliebste mein” (“I stand at the door, open for me and let me in, my dearest”).
	•	46r, parchment, 7.1 × 5.5 cm: Christ Child in a golden robe with a flower crown; from the backpack, scrolls with: lieb, frid, rainigkeit, diemutigkeit, gedult (love, peace, purity, humility, patience); inscription: “Ich Jhesus clarpring mit mir vil guetter jar und ain krenczlein das haist vergißnitmein” (“I Jesus bring with me many good years and a little wreath called ‘Forget-me-not’”).
	•	194v, paper, 4 × 6.2 cm: Christ Child in a tub between two plants, no inscription.
	•	206r, paper, 7.6 × 5.5 cm: Christ Child in a tub, with an angel beside him; inscription: “Ich hab vil zu hayß gepadet und bedorft daz man mich labet” (“I have wandered much in heat and need, that one may refresh me”).
	•	217r, parchment, ca. 6.3 × 5 cm: Christ Child with harp under flowers; above, in the scribe’s hand: “Ich Jesus wyl dyr wol und sues hofyern, das du dem fyeber mugst entpßyechen” (“I Jesus wish well and sweet joy to you, that you may withstand fever”).
	•	230r, parchment, 6.6 × 5 cm, tempera miniature on gold ground, differing from the other miniatures: a saint pouring medicine from a vessel into a sack for a nun; inscription: “Ich pin ein guoter arczt, wan ich gyb erczeney für den aussacz” (“I am a good doctor, for I give medicine for the plague”).
	•	261r, paper, 8 × 5.5 cm: Christ Child with backpack among vines; inscription: “Ich pin Jhs daz kindlein undprin (!) vil guter jar in meinem körblein” (“I am Jesus the little child, bringing many good years in my little basket”).
	•	264r, parchment, 6.5 × 6.1 cm: Christ with a lamb; inscription: “Durch die tieff meiner wunden hab ich das verloren schaff wider funden. Venite ad me” (“Through the depth of my wounds I have found again the lost sheep. Come to me”).

Three further miniatures are missing (glue traces on 51v, 244v, 275r). The images were originally planned to be part of the text. Cf. B. Hernad, Eine kuriose Christus-Darstellung in München, Zs. f. Kunstgeschichte 49 (1986), pp. 579–583, this manuscript p. 581.

Provenance: like Cgm 4473, evidently written by Eufrosina Gärtnerin for her own use; cf. the ownership note on fol. 269r and, on the inside of the back cover, an inscription in the hand of her sister Susanna:

“This little book belonged to Sister Eufrosina Gärtnerin, who died on the 12th day of the winter month in the year 1534, and afterwards it became Sister Susanna Gärtnerin’s. May almighty God grant them both grace here and eternally, amen. Pütrich Rule House.”

This book was written in the year when one counted from the birth of Christ 1493 by two sisters of the Order of Saint Clare of the convent at Söflingen, and the scribes request that one pray to God for them, whether they be living or dead, with a Pater noster or Ave Maria or Requiem aeternam. 1493. The names of these sisters (is crossed out) are Cordula von Reischach (the following d crossed out) and Cristina Keckin of Nuremberg.

According to the colophon (202vb), Fascicle I was written in 1493 by two sisters of the Poor Clares’ convent in Söflingen:

“This book was written in the year when one counted from the birth of Christ 1493 by two sisters of the Order of Saint Clare of the convent at Söflingen, and the scribes request that one pray to God for them, whether they be living or dead, with a Pater noster or Ave Maria or Requiem aeternam. 1493.”

In another script (loopless Bastarda), probably by a different contemporary hand, the sisters’ names are added:

“The names of these sisters (is crossed out) are Cordula von Reischach (the following d crossed out) and Cristina Keckin of Nuremberg.”

details.value: Das puch ward auSS geschriben an der helligen marter tag Johannes vnd Paulus tag als man zalt von Christus gepurt MCCCC. vnd ym L(X)XVII jar (erste X getilgt). Item das puch hot geschriben swester Hrabra Pfinczigin in Bilenrewt sancti Augustini ordinis regularium cananicarum czu lob vnd ere der ho"hsten trinitat vnd wer das nu"czt der gedenk ir gen got ym leben vnd todt was in got vermant etc.

This book was completed on the feast day of the Holy Martyrs John and Paul, according to the reckoning from the birth of Christ, 1500, and in the year L(X)XVII (the first X erased). Furthermore, this book was written by Sister Hrabra Pfinczigin in Bilenrewt, of the Order of Saint Augustine, Regular Canons, for the praise and glory of the Most Holy Trinity, and for the remembrance of her and her service to God in life and death, may she be united with God, etc.

(1r) das ist der erst vnd scholt vorn styn (getilgt); (13r) dis ist der ander sechstern vund geho"rt nach dem hernach (405v) des puchs ist als XXXV sechstern. THOSE ARE STRUCTURAL COMMENTS, THE BOOK IS BOUND IN SEXTERNS. Colophon (405v): Das puch ward auSS geschriben an der helligen marter tag Johannes vnd Paulus tag als man zalt von Christus gepurt MCCCC. vnd ym L(X)XVII jar (erste X getilgt). Item das puch hot geschriben swester Hrabra Pfinczigin in Bilenrewt sancti Augustini ordinis regularium cananicarum czu lob vnd ere der ho"hsten trinitat vnd wer das nu"czt der gedenk ir gen got ym leben vnd todt was in got vermant etc.

details.value: Zu lobe und erwurdikeit des almehtigen gottes ouch umb willen eins gemeinen nutzes der andechtigen swester des ordens sant marie magdalene sust genant der orden der ruwerin So hat geschriben dis buechelin Katherina Ingolt ein swester des selben ordens und conuentes zu strossburg mit irer hant grossem ernst flis und arbeit und hat daz volbroht mit der hilff gottes uff sant Thiburcius und valerianus tag Anno domini M cccc lxxxv

In praise and honor of Almighty God, and also for the common benefit of the devout sisters of the Order of Saint Mary Magdalene, also called the Order of the Penitents, this little book was written by Katherina Ingolt, a sister of this same order and convent in Strasbourg, with her own hand, with great diligence, effort, and labor. She completed it with God’s help on the feast day of Saints Tiburtius and Valerian, in the year of our Lord 1485.

details.value: f. 25r: Es ist zu wissen das die legend der heiligen wirdigen junckfrawn sant Margrethn nicht beslissung hat vmb des willen das si noch nicht erhaben ist ... Pittet got für vnsern erwirdigen getrewen liben vater vikari Jorg Valder der dise legend mit müe aus latein zu deüczsch pracht hat. Auch pitt ich euch mein allerherzigistn libsten muter vnd swester das ir got pittfür die schreiberinn s(wester) Agnes Pabnbergerin wann ich euch das mit ganzer begird meins herzen geschribn hab das ir mein dapei gedenkt zu got vnd der junckfrawn Maria mit einem avemaria. (Darunter von anderer Hand: gern gern.)

It should be known that the legend of the holy, worthy virgin Saint Margaret has no conclusion, because she has not yet been elevated [to sainthood]…
Pray to God for our venerable, faithful, dear father, Vicar Jörg Valder, who with effort has brought this legend from Latin into German.
I also beg you, my most beloved mother and sister, to pray to God for the scribe, Sister Agnes Pabnbergerin, for I have written this for you with the whole desire of my heart, so that you may remember me before God and the Virgin Mary with an Ave Maria.
(Underneath, in another hand: Gladly, gladly.)

Bound between 1448 and 1457 from two parts of different origins: Part I f. 1-120, brought by Kunigund Schreiber to the Monastery of St. Catherine in Nuremberg; Part II f. 121-259, brought by Katharina Tucher to the Monastery of St. Catherine in Nuremberg.

Red, often extensive headings, red lombard initials, pen flourishing. Often red ornamental curls at the upper and lower margins.
five pasted-in coloured woodcuts:
– fol. 44v, Schreiber II 817: Christ Child with flowers. 90 × 79 mm. Colours: carmine, vermilion, blue, ochre, and grey-brown. Upper Rhine, c. 1480. The Nuremberg copy not recorded by Schreiber.
– fol. 94r: Creation of Adam. Adam half reclining, half sitting diagonally to the right foreground; on the left God the Father with long hair and beard, wedge-shaped nimbus, long belted garment, reaching for Adam’s hands and eyes. In the background rocky terraces, one large and two small trees; in the foreground tufts of grass and two more small trees. Double frame 68 × 57 mm, trimmed without margins. Colours: strongly opaque green, blue, violet, and pink, with reserved highlights on God’s garment and Adam’s body. Not in Weinberger or Schreiber.
– fol. 98r: Man of Sorrows in half-figure with the instruments of the Passion, standing in the tomb; in front a pope and a cardinal in adoration. Christ, bearded head inclined to the left, with wedge-shaped nimbus, holding scourge and rod in crossed hands. Perspective tomb with four recesses; behind it a T-shaped cross with three nails, pillar of scourging, tongs, ladder, sponge on a reed, lance, hammer, and the thirty pieces of silver (?). In front of the tomb garments with three dice, a chalice and a cup (?). Double frame 71 × 61 mm, trimmed without margins. Colours: blue, violet, green, light ochre and grey-brown; nimbus and metal details silver, oxidised. Composition similar to Schreiber II 876, where Pilate and a mocker appear instead of pope and cardinal.
– fol. 101r, Schreiber I 721: Death of the Virgin. 67 × 57 mm. Colours: violet, blue, green, ochre, pale yellow; nimbi partly silver, oxidised.
– fol. 104r, Schreiber I 356: Carrying of the Cross. 67 × 56 mm. Colours: blue, green, light to medium brown; nimbi and metal details silver, oxidised.

The second hour of the evening had sounded on the glorious day of the conception of the humble Virgin, holy and blessed, who was free from original sin. On the eighth day of the last month I gave some rest to my weary pen, dry and clean, and the twentieth hour came forth alongside with upright mind. The year of our Lord 1455 was sounding when Maria daughter of Matteo the cloth-shearer finished copying the text and commentary of this poet, renowned and noble, and with a heart that sent its sparks as far as heaven. Praise the Lord, may He always be blessed.

Written in North-east France or possibly Cologne, as script and ornamentation in the type developed by the nuns of Chelles suggest; the MS has close affinity with the group of three MSS of St Augustine (Cologne, Dombibliothek 63, 65, 67) written by nuns for Hildebald, Archbishop of Cologne (785–819). (note: Jouarre was a double monastery, so these scribes could be women or men)
Origin North France, doubtless Chelles. The peculiar uncial and the decoration connect this MS with the group represented by the famous Sacramentary, Vatic. Regin. Lat. 316 (CLA 1.105). On f.1 is added in Anglo-Saxon script saec. VIII–IX Charlemagne's Letter to Abbot Baugulf of Fulda, and on f.260 a library catalogue, perhaps of Würzburg (see CLA plate). Belonged to St Kilian's of Würzburg certainly by the ninth century, as is shown by the entry on f.1v ('. . . faciat eum sancto Kiliano restitui'). The same page has the Würzburg ex-libris saec. XIII. Acquired by Archbishop Laud before 1638.
Ascribed to Chelles by Bischoff, to Jouarre by McKitterick.

details.value:
f.36v
Le ms. Français 1176 est un des vingt-cinq manuscrits entièrement copiés de la main de Christine de Pizan. Selon l’ Album Christine de Pizan, ce manuscrit est le plus ancien témoin du texte, daté de 1405. 

Corrections de la main de Christine de Pizan : additions indiquées dans la marge et rapportées dans l'interligne (f.58) ; additions avec signes de renvoi (f.20v, 43, 63) ; au f.76, préparation de la rubrique en écriture cursive. Nombreux mots, souvent déjà exponctués, barrés de rouge. Au verso de la 3e garde de parchemin, table de l'ouvrage ajoutée à l'encre rouge de la main de l'auteur.

Three signature systems: signatures in text ink consisting of a letter and a Roman numeral, signatures in graphite, signatures in black ink. Catchwords. A few holes (see folios 10, 23, 25, 29, 33), a few stains (see folios 2n, 25v, 55v), edge on folios 52 and 54. Rubricated chapter titles. Rubricated incipits and explicits. Latin quotations underlined in red ink (folios 13v, 15v, 16v, 67).

Decorated letters with phylacteries (fols. 13v, 33, 35v, 37v, 39, and passim) and cadels. Uniform dark brown ink for the main text; bright red for the rubrics. Rubrics and corrections are in the same hand as the principal text.

A semi-grisaille illumination, the width of one column, attributed to the Master of the Epistre d’Othéa, so named for his illustration in the copy made for Duke Jean de Berry (ms. BnF, Français 606). Christine de Pizan is depicted wearing a beige robe and a white cornette, seated in her study on a canopied chair, writing in a book at a table covered with pink cloth. The three coats of arms on either side of the window and beneath the arcade have been left blank.

The secondary decoration is by the ornamenter known as “aux brins de fantaisie”, who worked between 1403 and 1406 on eleven manuscripts produced in Christine de Pizan’s workshop.
Frame of gold and blue bands bordered with scrolling vines of blue and gold florets, with four gold bezants and four gold roundels, alternating with gold “hedgehog” leaves.
Framed initials (4 lines high) on gold grounds on fols. 1 and 25; with a blue phylactery wrapped vertically around the “I” introducing the text on fol. 1.
Champ initials (2 lines high) at the beginning of each chapter.
Champ paragraph marks (pieds-de-mouche).

details.value: Les manuscrits de Christine de Pizan ont été écrits par trois mains bien reconnaissables : P, R et X (Christine de Pizan elle-même). Le ms Français 835 a été transcrit, dans sa majeure partie par R, identifié à P. de Cruce : cf.Delsaux, « Profil d’un copiste des manuscrits originaux de Christine de Pisan : P. de La Croix, alias la main R », article à paraître dans Scriptorium. P a copié les ff.441vb, l. 26 à 44vb. La main X a fait quelques corrections : mouche ou restauration sur laquelle l’auteur a réécrit, à l’encre noire, les mots manquants au f.100 : cf.G. Ouy et C. Reno, « Identification des autographes de Christine de Pizan », dans Scriptorium, 34, 1980, p. 221-238.

Explicit Compendium Theologicae Virtutis (sic). We give thanks to God. Written by Henrietta in the year of our Lord 1356 (the name and date are difficult to read due to ink smudges).

Another mention of the copyist, in her own hand, is found in the upper margin of f.1r: Written by Henrietta of Lathilliaco, in the year 55 (not a clear reading), on Thursday after the feast of Saint Luke (22 October 1355).

The reasons for the transcription are explained on the same f.1r: Here begins the Compendium of Theology by Saint Thomas Aquinas, transcribed here interlinearly, so that the parchment may not remain idle.

value.title: Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, Latin 11969

details.value: Hugo Ripelin, Compendium theologicae veritatis, written between the lines and on the margins of a codex containing biblical texts from the 12th century. The space intended for the gloss, which was left blank, was occupied by the new text. The dimensions of the manuscript (ff.195) are 320x215 mm, the space for the original text is 208x90 mm for 18 lines on a full page. Many of the sheets were partially cut, presumably to make parchment. In 1354, before the new text was added, the codex had belonged to Nicasius, curate of 'Casiacum' (Chezy-sur-Marne, Aisne), as can be deduced from the ex libris on f.195v.The manuscript was later transferred to Saint-Germain-des-Prés (ex libris of the 16th century on f.195v and of the 18th century, with the signature 116, on the unnumbered sheet preceding f.1).

The original text has 18 lines, but the new text, copied by a woman has between 20 and 38 lines. It was copied a century after the original text, in spaces originally left for the gloss. Many sheets are partially cut.

The original text was in two columns and the ruling was done with leadpoint. It has catchwords but not signatures. The text block measures: 208x90mm.

details.value:
Des annotations et corrections interlinéaires sans doute de la main de la copiste : f.4r, 5r, 33r-34r, 39r, 42r, 44r, 46v-54r ; et d’autres mains : f.41r-43v, 47r-47v. Des annotations marginales de diverses mains : au f.1r, la cote Colbert, la cote Regius répétée deux fois, la cote actuelle, une ligne d’un chant religieux (« Nunctio uere quia misit dominus angelimi »), et des neumes (orisci catalans et neumes aquitains ; on en trouve aussi au f.54v) ; d’autres annotations à connotation religieuse sont à noter aux f.6r, 42v et 54v ; un certain nombre d’annotations sont illisibles ou effacées (f.11r, 22r, 40r et 54r) ; on peut également mentionner un astérisque au f.45r, un « y » au f.49r et, d’une main moderne, « 307 » sur le f.54v. 
Comme l’indiquent C. Jeudy (1974, p. 129-130) et B. Bischoff (2014, p. 128-129) dans leur notice respective, le manuscrit a été copié dans le troisième quart du IXe siècle en France, dans un scriptorium d’influence insulaire, par une copiste du nom d’Eugenia, qui donne son nom dans une souscription rédigée en lettres grecques (mais en langue latine) au f.54r (voir H. OMONT, 1905, p. 15 pour la transposition). Il a peut-être été copié dans le Sud de la France ou en Catalogne, ou du moins s’y est trouvé très vite après sa copie, car la main légèrement postérieure à la première (fin du IXe siècle) qui ajoute les carmina des f.54r et 54v est caractérisée par des traits wisigothiques et des neumes d’Aquitaine et orisci catalans ont été notés sur les f.1r et 54v vers la même période.

Quem scripsit Soror Wendelmodis Roltemans ad instanciam carissime neptis eius Leve Ter Bruggen honeste matrone. Et Soror Agnes Martini illuminavit. f.184v-185r: "This little prayer book was completed in the year of our Lord 1478, on the very day of Saint Ambrose the Bishop. It was written by Sister Wendelmodis Roltemans at the request of her dear niece Leve Ter Bruggen, an honorable matron. And Sister Agnes Martini illuminated it. The holy nuns of the monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict at Saint Catherine in Syloe, near the renowned and prosperous city of Groningen in Friesland. Johanna (Jeanne) von Mörsberg may be regarded either as the scribe of this manuscript or as its commissioner, since tůn schriben can also mean “to have [something] written.” A Poor Clare at the convent of Gnadenthal in Basel, she became, in 1430, a penitent at St Mary Magdalene in the convent “An den Steinen,” where she died in 1450 (?) details.value: Questo libro si è scrito per mane/ de Lana de i Galvagni,/ fiola che fu de miser zan / Bertolameo. (Iesu) Maria.
This book was written by the hand of Lana de i Galvagni, daughter of the late Sir Zan Bertolameo. Jesus Mary.

f.219v, written on a fragment in Lana’s hand: “Franciscus / et Claram” centered, then below, “Questo libro si è scrito per mane/ de Lana de i Galvagni,/ fiola che fu de miser zan / Bertolameo. (Iesu) Maria.”

Rome, Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale, Varia 24 (574)
Lana dei Galvagni is not self-identified as a nun – but the contents of the ms. point to that conclusion – especially the “Regula perfecte religionis”. It was sent to a “Fra Giustino romano cappuccino predicatore” from Venice (f.218r). Lana states her name as “Lana de Galvagni fiola che fu de miser zan Bertolameo” (f.219v) – is this the Venetian Zuan? If so, this would again point to its production as Venetian. Lana wrote “Franciscus et Claram” on f.219v – was she possibly from a house of Clarissans? The ms. came from the Augustinian convent of Gesù e Maria in Rome

Due to the rebinding of the manuscript in the 17th/18th century, the original quire structure is no longer clearly discernible. The modern foliation skips one leaf after fol. 116 and does not take into account the new front and back flyleaves. The soiling of fols. 106r–110v and the change of scribe at fol. 106r suggest that the final part of the manuscript was added to the codex only at the time of rebinding. During this process, fol. 107 was incorrectly sewn: it should in fact follow fol. 118.

Decoration: Red headings, underlining, and emphasis strokes; from fol. 106r onward paragraph marks. Mostly two-line Lombard initials with simple floral ornament and tendril work. On fols. 1r, 43r, and 75r: six-, seven-, and four-line Lombard initials on a floral ground with light brown acanthus-leaf tendrils ending in multicolored blossoms, extending into the upper and outer margins.

details.value: A treshaute et puissante Princesse Elizabeth Roine d'Angleterre et cetera, Madame, combien que ie soye peu exercée ... De votre Majestie La treshumble, tresobeissante et tresaffectionnée servante a Jamais, Esther Langlois, Fille Françoise. Explicit: de pouvoir a Jamais vous faire treshumble service. Huius ipsius Libelli Prosopopoeia, Filia me scripsit mandante vtroque Parente/ Exilii calamo taedia discutiens.
Crown atop an unidentifiable device, hidden in the gutter on f.i only.
Collation beginning with f. ii: 12 24 34(replacement leaf attached to stub of original 3rd leaf) 42 5-124 136 142(+ a leaf pasted to 2nd leaf)

To the most high and powerful Princess Elizabeth, Queen of England, etc., Madam, although I am little practiced… From Your Majesty’s most humble, most obedient, and most affectionate servant forever, Esther Langlois, a French daughter.”

Explicit: “To be forever able to render you most humble service. The personification of this very little book — my daughter wrote me, at the command of both parents / driving away the tedium of exile with her pen.”

f.325:
“The Epistles were translated by the venerable and spiritual Master Hans Amman from Weissenau near Rafelspuerkch for the spiritual virgins and sisters at the Himmelspforten convent in Vienna, where he served as prior for more than twenty years. May God be gracious to his soul. The Epistles were later copied by Sister Magdalena, whom Almighty God and His beloved Mother Mary hold in their care.”

f.360:
“In the year of our Lord 1468, on the Feast of the Conception of Our Lady, during Advent, this book was completed. It belongs to the Himmelspforten convent in Vienna and was written by Sister Magdalena Panholezin. Pray to God for her with an Ave Maria. Thanks be to God.”
The main scribe Magdalena Panholczin and a second scribe also named Magdalene, are both mentioned in damaged text on f 360r.

Part of C08 was written in the years 1473–1486, when Margareta Claesdotter was abbess. The name of the scribe cannot be determined here in a fully objective manner. In the second part, the name of the scribe is certain, but the dating is not sufficiently precise. However, in 1486 Anna Fickesdotter became prioress, and this would probably have been mentioned in some way if the manuscript had been written after that year. There is, however, no doubt that the hand is the same in both parts. Kristina Johansdotter Brask wrote the directorium chori.

The Schelm von Bergen family of Wildenberg provided two Cistercian nuns for the convent of Seligental in the 15th–16th c.: Magdalena (attested 1464–1471) and Amalie, d. 1561 as the last abbess (M. details.value:
Writer of the main parts: Sister Barbara von Rottenburg in the Dominican monastery Maria-Reut(h)in (Fiala/Irtenkauf p. 84)
Based on the documents used for binding, this (collective) manuscript originates from the Dominican convent of Reutin. According to G. Piccard’s watermark analysis, it was not begun before 1515 and was completed by around 1529.
The main scribe of its primary sections is Sister Barbara von Rottenburg of Reutin (Gand No. 175), who identifies herself in a manuscript she authored (Cod. theol. et phil. oct. 31, f.64r). She is considered the primary scribe of Reutin from around 1488 to 1534. Her works include:
• Cod. theol. et phil. qu. 77 (1488-1492),
• Cod. theol. et phil. oct. 31 (1492),
• Cod. brev. 27 (1511),
• Cod. brev. 73 (1521),
• Cod. theol. et phil. qu. 49a-b (1524),
• Cod. brev. 49 (1529),
• Cod. theol. et phil. oct. 33 (1534).

details.value: Explicit hoc opus psalterii per me Barbaram Gretzingerin de Lindow conventualem monasterii nomine Berg anno domini milesimo (sic) quadringentesimo quinquagesimo quarto
This work of the Psalter is completed by me, Barbara Gretzingerin of Lindow, a convent member of the monastery named Berg, in the year of our Lord one thousand four hundred and fifty-four.
219 r: Explicit hoc opus psalterii per me Barbaram Gretzingerin de Lindow conventualem monasterii nomine Berg anno domini milesimo (sic) quadringentesimo quinquagesimo quarto

Numerous cadels (penwork initials)
* Numerous small fleuronné initials
* 13 large decorated initials

Initials for antiphons and versicles:

Each begins with a one-line-high initial (covering a four-line musical staff + text), usually in a rectangular form:

* Black cadel with a red central stroke
* Left side: looped “rucksack-like” extension
* Interior fields: left in parchment tone, filled with acanthus-like or ornamental motifs, often with hatched areas
* Frequently includes heads or half-figures on the far left
* Right side: contour line with regularly spaced groups of three or four pearls

Psalm Initials

* Psalms begin with mostly 3-line red Lombard initials (rarely 2 lines)
* Decorated with similar contour lines and internal acanthus motifs
* Interiors sometimes highly abstract
* Frequent use of hatched areas

⸻

Major Decorated Initials (12 Psalms)

Unusually, 12 psalms are marked with large (4–9 line) decorated initials:

* Some correspond to liturgical divisions:
    * Psalms 1, 26, 38, 68, 109 → liturgical eightfold division
    * Psalms 51, 101 → Gallican division
* Others (21, 45, 59, 73, 85) do not match known systems

Color schemes:

* Mostly blue-red initials
* One red-green split initial (56r) with stamped or toothed cut-out shapes
* Others: monochrome blue initials

Interior decoration:

* Checkerboard and stripe patterns dominate
* Checkerboards filled with:
    * floral motifs (cross-flowers, star-flowers)
    * diamonds and triangles in alternating red/blue
* Stripe patterns composed of acanthus vines
* Complex geometric arrangements (e.g. Psalm 73: symmetrical grid; Psalm 59: combined pattern system)

⸻

Figural Elements

* Two initials (71r, 86r) contain monster figures in the letter body or interior field
* Example: a large blue fleuronné initial P (206v) with acanthus-filled interior (Office of the Dead)

⸻

Border Decoration

* No uniform system
* Contour lines sometimes form rectangular frames
* Spandrels filled with:
    * acanthus
    * floral stems
    * geometric squares
* Occasional floral extensions and leaf clusters
* Rare use of bud-fleuronné (e.g. Psalm 1)

details.value: 19 fleuronné initials (with pen drawing). The 14 main sections of the first text (summary, introduction, one for each of the 12 brothers) begin with 8- to 13-line red initials, the inner fields of which all contain short tendrils with differently lobed leaves in black outline and sparse internal drawing on a red cross-hatched background (1 ra top, 1 vb , 39 ra ), with the exception of the D on 84 rb , which is filled with a sheaf of buds. Occasionally, grotesque faces in profile appear opposite each other (67 ra ). Star blossoms and S-ornaments with thickened ends are usually left out of the letter bodies, but profile leaves and trifoliate leaves are also occasionally included (26 vb ). The spandrels of the rectangular frames made of narrow strips with short curved sections are often filled with trifoliate and small motifs, occasionally also on cross-hatching. The frame moldings and the left shafts may be decorated with arched friezes (26 vb , 39 ra ) and frequently, at intervals, with short, fan-shaped bundles of rays. Some initials have downward extensions, usually short, consisting of rows of tapering beads bordered by thin lines (1 ra , 1 vb , 39 ra ).

Bilingual – Latin and Middle Dutch – psalter (Den Haag, Koninklijke Bibliotheek, MS 133 C 1) - The psalms are supplemented by both a prayer in Dutch and one in Latin, and by a Latin commentary which is derived from Ludolf von Sachsen’s Expositio super psalterium.15 According to the renowned Flemish philologist Jan Deschamps, Elisabeth did not translate the Latin texts into Middle Dutch herself; supposedly she used a Brabantine redaction of a West-Flemish translation of the psalter, which was made at the end of the thirteenth or the beginning of the fourteenth century. Nevertheless, the fact that Elisabeth gathered texts from different sources and put them together shows that she must have had excellent Latin.16

details.value: Summus honor celi / Filius ipse ipse pater / Hoc opus explerunt / Inde sibi veniam / Qui te sustulerit / spes grata Maria fideli / remanes in virgine mater / Aleith Claricia querunt / te venerando piam / hunc anathema ferit.
Mater Ide Lifmundis fecit hec scribi. anima eius requiescat in pace.

The greatest honor of heaven,
the Son Himself, the Father Himself,
completed this work.
From Him, may forgiveness
be given to whoever carries you.
O gracious hope, Mary faithful,
you remain a virgin mother.
Aleith and Claricia seek you,
venerating you, O pious one.
This [text] invokes a curse upon [him who acts against it].
Mother Ida Lifmund had this written. May her soul rest in peace.

details.value: Zu lob und er got dem almachtigen, Marie und allen heiligen und dem menschen zu underweisung, und aus haissen der erwirdigen geistleichen frawn Ludmille, priorin, meiner lieben muetter und frawn, ich swester Barbara, verluepte der regel sand Augustin und der ordnung und statutt Praemonstratensium zu Pernekch, hab geschriben das gegenwuertig puech mit aygner hant, das gemacht und gepredigt hat der hach gelert maister Gorig zu Wien, und ich hab das volentt an dem nagsten tag nach Colomanni des heiligen m[artyre]r. Die schreiberin pitt zu lan ain Ave Maria umb ir meue die sy hat gehabt mit dem schreiben

To praise and give glory to Almighty God, to Mary, and to all the saints, and for the instruction of humanity, and from the desire of the venerable spiritual lady Ludmille, prioress, my dear mother and lady, I, Sister Barbara, devoted to the rule of St. Augustine and to the order and statutes of the Premonstratensians at Pernegg, have written this present book with my own hand, which was composed and preached by the highly learned Master Gorig at Vienna, and I completed it on the next day after the feast of St. Coloman the martyr. The scribe asks you, as an act of charity, to say an Ave Maria for her soul, for the effort she put into writing.

In the year of our Lord one thousand four hundred and eighty-six, Sister Beatris Dircs, daughter of Bonen, wrote this little book when she was sixty-two years old and had lived in the cloister for forty-five years. Pray for her for God's sake, and recite a Our Father and three Hail Marys.

details.value: f.111v: "Inden jaer ons heren doemen screef M iiii[c] ende lxxxvi soe heeft suster beatris dircs bonen dochter dit boecskijn ghescreven Doe si out was lxii jaer Ende ghewoent hadde in den cloester xlv jaer Bidt voer hoer om godswille Ende leest een pater noster ende iii ave maria."

Whereas according to the Byvanck database, this manuscript may have been made in the eastern part of the Northern Netherlands, according the Database BNM, it was made in Amstelland
Provenance
The manuscript was written by a certain Beatris Dircs Bonen dochter for a convent of Canonesses Regular, dedicated to St. Nicholas and St. Mary Magdalene. According to the Database BNM, the formula on f.17r-17v suggests that the manuscript was made for the Canonesses Regular of St. Mary Magdalene (Op het Spui), Amsterdam. According to Stooker & Verbeij (1997), the formula could have also been for the Canonesses Regular of St. Mary Magdalene, Zaltbommel.

The decoration is rich and carefully executed:
	•	On f. 1r, the page is framed and contains a decorated initial; within the frame is a small miniature of St Augustine holding the civitas Dei.

	•	Large foliate initials on gold backgrounds open major sections.
	•	Smaller initials in blue and red are filigreed in red and purple.
	•	Paragraph marks are in blue and red; titles and running titles are written in red ink.

details.value: f.302: An dem 1316 iar von christes gebort. Is ditz büch erzüget. Von der hoch-geborn vrowen Elzebeten der werden zwire kuninginnen. zu einem ewigen zügnisse iris namen und allers geschlechtes fürsten und kunige om welch closter ditz büch wirt gegeben daz men ir da ewicliche gedenke zum ersten der di da tot sin daz di slafen in Gotes fride und zu der exigen freude kumen. di da noch leben daz sich die freuwen selde und lanklebens; der nach-kümelinge daz si in tusent geslechte wachsen. Amen.

“In the year 1316 after the birth of Christ, this book was produced by the noble lady Elisabeth, descendant of two illustrious queens, as an eternal testament to her name and that of her entire lineage of princes and kings. Whichever monastery receives this book, may she be eternally remembered there. First, for those who are deceased, may they rest in God’s peace and come to eternal joy. For those who are still living, may they enjoy happiness and long life. For their descendants, may they flourish for a thousand generations. Amen.”

details.value: Mostly watermarks already known from other St Catherine manuscripts: 	•	Characteristic ox-head types in various forms, including: 	•	Ox-head with eyes and nostrils, with staff and “Z” (e.g. fol. 3), as in Codd. sang. 363 and 1916 (here: right eye placed higher, right ear hanging downward, right cheek indented). 	•	Mitre-like mark (fol. 4), as in Codd. sang. 363, 406, 1916. 	•	Small crown (from fol. 19 onward), as in Cod. sang. 1066. 	•	Female head (from fol. 106 onward), as in the Urbar register booklet. Watermarks not previously attested in other St Catherine manuscripts: 	•	Small, somewhat misshapen ox-head (fols. 66–69), visible especially on fol. 67, somewhat similar to Piccard II/2 (1966), VII, no. 226 (Basel, Strasbourg 1489), though that model has a staff with star as subsidiary mark (possibly here not visible?); not recorded in Briquet. 	•	Chalice (fol. 135; clearly visible fols. 155 and 167), very similar to Briquet no. 4546 (Sion 1490; Lucerne 1492; Freiburg im Breisgau 1494). 	•	Toward the end: large crown (lower part visible fol. 175; upper part fol. 180). Watermarks allow only approximate chronological placement (1480s), not precise dating.

Principal compiler’s hand: Angela Varnbühler
	•	Initially writes in her characteristic, disciplined, formal Bastarda.
	•	From 1481 onward alternates with the hand of Elisabeth Muntprat.
	•	Over the years she continues to add entries passim.
	•	Her script develops into a more right-leaning, less formal semi-cursive.
	•	Her last autograph entry concerns the year 1505 (written at age 64).
	•	In the final years before her death (1509), she no longer writes herself but dictates to a fellow sister (entries fol. 106r [1505], 109r [1506], 113r [1507]). Entries mentioning “mine[m] lieben vetter hansen varnbueler” are certainly not in her hand.

Additional identifiable scribal hands
	•	Cordula von Schönau (fols. 70v–71v)
	•	Justina Blarer (fols. 86r; 87r–88v; 96v–97r; 111v–114v; and elsewhere)
	•	Sapientia Wirt
	•	Elisabeth Schaigenwiler (fols. 132v–143v)
	•	Regula Keller (fols. 102r–v; 115v ff.; 152r–v; 154r–157r; 158r–161r; 160r–v; 162v–164r; 169r ff.; 175v; 185r)
Lines and text block size are variable.

After the council of the city of St. Gallen lifted the enclosure of the Dominican monastery of St. Catherine on May 2, 1528, and the convent gradually dissolved, only Regula Keller and two sisters remained in the monastery buildings, where she continued to copy the Rule of Augustine and the Constitutions of the Order of Preachers until 1543. The reading of the Rule and Constitutions was emphasized more strongly in Reformed monasteries, in keeping with the nature of the Observance. (men)

records.rec_Title: Wil, Dominikarinnenkloster St. Katharina, Schwesternbuch; Full manuscript

details.value:
Schwesternbuch, Sisters' book
The designation “Schwesternbuch” is misleading.

It does not correspond to what scholarship usually calls a “Sisters’ Book,” namely:

“a seemingly chronicle-like compilation of numerous short vitae of deceased sisters of a particular convent, produced by members of the subsequent generation of sisters” (Ringler, 1980, p. 4).

The St Gall Schwesternbuch shares with that genre:
	•	a chronicle-like character (Part I)
	•	gradual textual expansion
	•	didactic and edifying function (Part II)

However, it should not, as has unfortunately happened in older scholarship, be misinterpreted—especially in its second part—as a document presenting exemplary traditions of spiritual life at St Katharina, St Gall.

That literary type arose in the first half of the 14th century as a female counterpart to the Vitas fratrum (see Meyer, Katharinental, 1995, p. 23).

value.title: Lamspringe, Benedictine, Lamspringe, Lower Saxony, Germany,-1138

details.value:
6 initials. 1 miniature. Two marginal drawings.
Miniature: On 1v, at the beginning of the Bede text, a colored pen drawing of a scribe working at a lectern (framed). In his hands he holds a knife and a pen. On the lectern are an open book and inkwells. Kneeling, a monk/cleric (possibly a provost of Lamspringe) holds the shaft of the lectern in his arms. Within the frame, around the drawing, is the inscription: Ut huius sancti Hieronimi beatitudinis particeps apud dominum efficiatur, prefiguratus felix Petrus idcirco, quantum humana possibilitas permittit, eius doctrinis et meritis divina gratia preveniente incessanter adheret . 13.1–7.6 cm – framed field.

Initials: The initials at the beginnings of the texts around Bede (2r, 2v, 4r, 48v, 90v, and 129v) are cleft-frame initials with loosely curved spiral tendrils and five-pointed nailed clasps. The terminals are decorated with bulbous and palmette leaves. The latter sometimes show seeds, veins, and hatched leaf spines. The tendril forks have plastic (cf. 4r) and linear compressions. On 90v, the initial stem ends in a mythical creature's head. 2.2–5.4 cm.

Marginal drawings on the lower edges of the leaves: 136v a palmette plant. 139r, a colored pen drawing of a man in a cloak (a nobleman), holding a branch in his right hand. Beside him, a two-headed bird with branches in its beaks. Above, the inscription Filius columbae .P. porta[n]s [?] ramum oliviae (Gen 8:11) scilicet viscera misericordiae (Lc 1:78). Next to the bird, the inscription Vox turturis (with neumes). On the upper edge of leaf 35r, a head with a Phrygian cap (blind drawing). 139v: 3.0 × 4.4 cm (entire image area).

Colors: The initials are drawn with a red pen. Details (clasps and leaves) are washed in yellow. Garments are painted with light washes (orange and green). The valleys of folds are in a darkened local color, the highlights are left unpainted in parchment. The flesh tones are parchment-colored with circular red cheeks. The edges of the garments, the shaft of the lectern, as well as the cushions and bench are ornamentally decorated in orange and washed in yellow. The miniature and border drawing on 139r are in the same color scheme.
