Signatures on the foot of the last verso page of the following gathers: (8v): Ius , (32v): IIIIus , (40v) : Vus , (48v): VIus , (64v): VIIIus and (80v): Xus , otherwise lost due to trimming.
single column (1v, 25rv, 49rv, 83rv, 114v two columns)

Rubricated, the rubrics are written in uncial mixed with rustic capitals. In addition, larger red and green uncial capitals alternate as a display script in the first lines of text. At the beginning of each book, split-bar initials with a white, red-outlined bar (decorated with alternating red and green dots), nailed buckles, and red gap filling, accompanied by foliate tendrils in the center, their vegetal elements highlighted in relief by red dashes. The cushion background of the initials is alternately green and blue in sections; smaller areas are also highlighted in gold, as are the buckles and some of the terminal bulbous leaves. 2r, initial S over 13 lines with green gap filling. The letter ends are formed as dog or dragon heads, from which tendrils with half-palmettes grow, filling the center and featuring palmettes or acanthus-like profile leaves as terminal motifs; two further, similarly decorated tendrils are attached directly to the letter body with buckles. 26r, initial QOver 14 lines, with a red gap fill, blue background of the outer frame, inner field filled with green and gold (padded ground). The figure, extending diagonally across the entire width of the text area, is designed as an elongated, two-legged dragon with red-gold outlines and a green-red dotted body, whose tail terminates in a vegetal ornament (a fan-like trefoil consisting of two conical leaves and a central acanthus leaf). The creature's neck is coiled in a knot around the letter stem; from the mouth of its head, which extends into the inner field, emerges a double, axially symmetrical tendril with half-palmette and bud leaves, filling the inner field and extending beyond it to the left. 50r, initial P over 16 lines against a green-blue padded ground. The stem of the letter grows downwards from the mouth of a frontally depicted lion's head and consists of two parallel gold border bands, which terminate at the bottom in a braided knot and terminate in two tendrils with terminal red bulbous leaves. The stem is filled with a frieze-like ornament consisting of slanted red half-palmettes and green acanthus leaves in alternating sequence. The head of the letter consists of a red-filled cleft strip into which a dog-like creature, rearing up on its hind legs against the stem, extends its head. From the creature's mouth grows a short-stemmed tendril adorned with various leaf shapes. 84r, initial P over 16 lines against a green-blue cushioned background, cleft fillings gold with a red diamond grid. The head of the P terminates in a tendril adorned with half-palmettes and bulbous leaves, which fills the central field. A tendril winds its way to the bottom of the initial, upon which sits a stylized bird whose beak bites the border. From the upper joint grows a short, outward-curving tendril with a downward-pointing dog's or dragon's head, from whose mouth emerges a cone-shaped golden figure decorated with a red lattice and green dots. 114v, initial Q over 9 lines on a green field, the inner field alternating green and blue, the cleft fillings red, the buckles gold. The cauda, ​​formed as a vegetal cleft border, shows a gold cleft filling with a red diamond lattice and flower, terminating in a strongly lobed half-palmette. The inner field is filled with two axially symmetrical half-palmette tendrils, the ends of which are curled in a volute-like fashion and also wrapped around the letter stem; both are fastened with buckles. Such split-border initials with varying colored backgrounds and diverse vegetal tendril forms are characteristic of the codices of the "Scriptrix Group"

On the lower margin of fols. 8v, 16v, and 24v, quire signatures in Arabic numerals I–III (III on 24v); on the lower margin of the last verso of the next seven quires, quire signatures in minuscule letters a–g. The quires from fol. 96 onward mostly have red catchwords.

•	1v: an initial I spanning 13 lines, shaped like a chalice that widens upward like a funnel or flower, with four budding “knob-leaf” offshoots attached to the body with buckle-like bands (identical in Cod. Guelf. 475 Helmst., 175v). From the leafy chalice emerges the haloed St Augustine (bust) with crozier, book (?) and mitre (illustrated in Cohen-Mushlin, 166 no. 145). Executed only as an outline drawing; the depiction resembles the fully finished initial in Cod. Guelf. 204 Helmst., 3v.
	•	27r: inhabited column-bar initial D over 5 lines, in uncial form, with a tail ending in knob-leaf forms. In the inner field, Bede appears as a haloed tonsured monk (bust), writing with a pen in his right hand while holding a penknife/correcting knife in his left to steady the leaf. Also only outlined.
	•	On 25v, 88r, and 106r, space was left for initials; on 126r an initial O is outlined as a red circle.

The initials were probably executed—like those in Cod. Guelf. 475 Helmst.—by the scribe and illuminator Ermengarde.

value.title: Wolfenbüttel, Herzog August Bibliothek, Cod. Guelf. 502 Helmst.

details.value:
The inside of the front cover and the endpaper contain fragments of a manuscript similar to the Graduale, the back dirt page belonged to a lectionario or breviario from the 14th century and the inside of the back cover is covered with a fragment of a liturgical parchment manuscript, also from the 14th century. At the foot of this fragment is written:
Qui scripsit, scribat et longo tempore vivat. Amen.
Que me scribebat, Sophia nomen habebat. Explicitly liber iste.

During the period in which the Hs. was created, four bearers of this name have been handed down among the Marienberg choir women: the sexton Sophia Barnstorf and the conventual nuns Sophia von Braunschweig , Sophia von Werle and Sophia von Meinersen 
Around 1510, the Graduale was supplemented (Part II) and then re-bound after identifying the scribe's hand and the binding stamp in the Benedictine monastery of Clus in accordance with the requirements of the reformed liturgy of the Bursfeld Benedictine Congregation. 

In the catalogue of Colophons of the Bouveret, noted as wolfenbüttel 542.

Signatures in Roman numerals on the lower margin of the last verso page of each quire: I–XXII.
At the rebinding, the text sequence of the final quires was disturbed; the correct leaf order is: 221r–255v, 259r–266v, 269r–v, 256r–258v, 267r–v.

Numerous historiated initials in body color and fleuronnée initials by four hands.
Hand 1: At the beginning of the offices for feasts of the Lord, historiated initials in body color of varying size (each 1–3 lines of text and music) on gold ground framed by alternating red and blue bars. Letter bodies in uncial form in light violet purple with gray contours and dot patterns; ascenders and descenders end outside the frame in winding terminals with a scarcely differentiated red or green half-palmette leaf. 1v initial A over 3 lines of text and music for the proper of the first Sunday of Advent. The letter body is formed by two two-legged dragons in light purple with blue wings, set axially symmetrically opposite each other, whose necks intertwine above Christ enthroned (Maiestas domini). Christ, with red nimbus, is clothed in a purple undergarment and a blue pallium; he holds a book in the left hand, the right raised in blessing. He sits frontally on a white throne into whose sides the two dragons clutch. In the upper spandrels between letter body and frame are the evangelist symbols of Matthew (man, left) and John (eagle, right); the heads of the lion of Mark and the bull of Luke are inserted into the intertwined tails of the two dragons. 8r initial D over 2 lines of text and music for the office of the Christmas Vigil: in the inner field an angel clothed in brown announces the birth of Christ to a shepherd in a red garment who pastures his sheep on green meadow ground. 10r initial P over 3 lines of text and music for the office of the Christmas Mass: before a stylized stable architecture, over whose roof ox and ass look out, Mary, resting on a white couch, in blue undergarment and red outer garment, holds up the infant Jesus wrapped in light-blue linen; Joseph, identified by a red mantle and Jew’s hat, regards the scene from the right. 48v initial D over 2 lines of text and music for the Palm Sunday office: in the center Christ, wearing a blue undergarment and red pallium, enters Jerusalem from the right on a gray ass. Two inhabitants of the city scatter palm branches or have climbed into a tree waving. 55v initial T over one line of text and music for the washing of the feet with Crucifixion scene, the Crucified himself forming the letter T. 61r initial ligature VD over 3 lines of text and music for the Easter procession: from the left come the three Marys in red and blue garments with ointment vessels to the tomb of Christ, where they are addressed by an angel clothed in white, winged red, and nimbed, standing on green ground with black shading. 67r initial P over 3 lines of text and music for the trope of Easter morning Postquam factus est homo: Christ, clothed in blue undergarment and red pallium and armed with a cross-banner, breaks open the gates of hell, represented as the gaping, toothed maw of a monster with blazing flames, and draws Adam out of the chasm. 76v initial V over 2 lines of text and music for the office of the Ascensio domini: the representation follows the type of the disappearing Christ; Mary (left) and Peter (right), together with five further apostles, surround a grass-covered hill on which the footprints of Christ are visible, while the upper half of the Son of God has already disappeared into a blue wavy cloud band. 77v initial S over 2 lines of text and music for the Pentecost office: in the lower part of the letter field sit, in traditional representation, Mary and the apostles in red, green, and blue garments, while from above the Holy Spirit descends upon them in the form of a dove. Similar decoration is also found in the Marienberg liturgical manuscripts Cod. Guelf. 145.1 Helmst. (mentioned by Härting, 15), 1312 Helmst., and 309 Novi. —
Hand 2: 65v marginal narrative representation of Christ’s descent into hell: Christ, clothed in a blue undergarment and red pallium and armed with a cross-banner, breaks open the gates of hell, represented as the gaping, toothed maw of a monster with blazing flames, and leads Adam and Eve upward. Although the coloring in particular corresponds to the miniatures of the first hand, the rendering of garments and folds, and especially of flesh tones and faces, differ considerably. 67r body-color initial R over 5 lines of text and music for the high feast of the Resurrection: Christ, clothed in blue undergarment and red pallium and armed with a cross-banner, rises from his opened tomb, facing the viewer frontally and raising the right hand in blessing. Before the box-like sarcophagus, two guards armored with chain-mail shirts, surcoats, and iron hats, and armed with spears, are sunk in sleep. —
Hand 3: 53v body-color initial N over one line each of text and music for the gradual responsory in coena domini (CANTUS 505005): on golden background framed with a thin black line stands the red uncial letter without any decoration. In the inner field kneels Christ clothed in dark red garment, with cross-nimbus. —
Hand 4: 59v fleuronnée initial I over the entire height of the text area for the hymn of the blessing of the Easter candle in the Easter Vigil (AH 50 no. 31 st. 1–4, 7 [modified], 9–12): the letter itself is colored red and furnished with bands running parallel from top to bottom in wavy meanders in black, white, and light red tones. It evidently represents the Paschal candle itself, at whose top a bell-shaped container is attached, to which the Holy Spirit in the form of a white dove brings fire from above. The contours of the letter body are furnished with delicate blue fleuronnée ornament in the form of parallel thread-like extensions, buds, notched pearls, and fibrils extending upward and downward to the edge of the page. 60v fleuronnée initial E over two lines each of text and music for the Exultet: the letter body, divided red and blue in complex stamp-like patterns, is filled in the two parts of the inner field separated by crossbars with delicate red vines, growing axially symmetrically from vase-like vessels and ending in round medallions filled with bud-spikes. The letter body is enclosed in a blue frame with bud-fleuronnée, which, like the borders extending over the entire height of the text area, is filled with bud-fleuronnée and set with pearls and fibrils. The upper and lower end of the border are decorated with delicate leaf and floral motifs. — Rubricated, mostly red display majuscules with blue contour strokes, together with others (mostly at the beginning of the sequence strophes and in the Kyriale) executed in cadel-like black and red. At the beginning of the individual offices, alternating red and blue fleuronnée initials with variously curving thread-like extensions and simple ornament of buds and pearls as well as fibrils in the contrasting color. Line fillers in various wave and zigzag forms.
Above each text line a five-line staff with c- and f-clef, c-line yellow, f-line red, with a mixed form of Metz and Gothic chant notation by various hands.

details.value: Rubricated, red Lombards, marginal corrections and additions framed in red, scriptural quotations underlined in red. Section majuscules in black, depending on the letter form stroked, dotted, or filled in red. At the beginning of the individual books, column-staff initials with white staff stem outlined in red, clasps, and red column filling, colored grounds and frames. In detail: 73r (preface to book I), initial I over 9 lines, through the slit in the letter stem winds a dragon outlined in red; the letter is framed left blue, right green, each with red dots. 78r (book I), initial F over 10 lines on a framing ground blue on the left and green on the right with red dots, surrounded by a red wavy line. The vertical shaft of the F is formed of two spirally interlaced staffs outlined in green; one ends above in a leafy curved branch and below in a serpent’s head; the ends of the second are identical but reversed. From the upper serpent’s head grows the body of a winged dragon forming the upper crossbar of the letter; from its mouth protrudes a human foot. The second crossbar of the F is a simple column-staff separating two inner-field motifs: in the upper part, the filius regis named in the text, in pen drawing as a crowned bust in speaking gesture with an open book; in the lower part, a dog-like beast of prey, from whose jaws grows a vine with knobbed and herb leaves as well as half-palmettes. Enlarged illustration in Härtel, 48. 98v (preface to book II), initial P over 16 lines, plain form with a knobbed-leaf vine in the field and a contour-following half-palmette vine; letter framed in gold color, only under the stem blue, as also the ground of the inner field. 99r (book II), similarly framed initial I over 9 lines, whose letter body is formed by two symmetrically intertwined serpents. 129v (preface to book III), initial E over 6 lines, framed in gold, inner field blue above and in front, green below, and at the clasp of the crossbar two axially symmetrical spiral vines with vegetal outgrowths. 129v (book III), initial D over 9 lines, framed in gold, inner field blue on the left, green on the right, with the crowned half-figures of Sponsus (left, with red scroll) and Sponsa (right), enlarged illustration in Härtel, 49. 137r (preface to book IV), initial P over 12 lines, analogous in design to the above, though here the ground is three-colored (gold, blue, green), and a bird additionally sits on the vine in the inner field. 137v (book IV), initial V over 11 lines with three-colored ground and framing (gold, blue, green); the inner field is occupied by the forepart of a lion shown from the side, looking backward, whose hindpart with tail wound through the hind legs projects far left into the side margin. From its mouth grows a vine with knobbed leaves and half-palmette.

details.value: a.d. etc. etc. (14)56 completus est liber iste per me sororem inutilem Alheydem Kalves religiosam ac professam in monasterio Stederborch. pro quo sit Deus benedictus in secula. “In the year 1456, this book was completed by me, Sister Alheydem Kalves, an useless religious and professed in the monastery of Stederborch. For which may God be blessed forever. Have patience, for I have written poorly in my 73rd year with great labor in the convent of Wynhusen during the expulsion of our monastery. Pray to God for me, one angelic greeting or eternal rest in the love of Christ.”

value.title: Wolfenbüttel, Herzog August Bibliothek, Cod. Guelf. 518a Helmst.

details.value:
The expulsion of the Steterburg convent (or part of it) to the Cistercian monastery of Wienhausen, mentioned by the writer, is not documented in any other historiographical or documentary sources.
The liturgical texts following the Windesheim custom and the Commemorationes of the house and order patrons James, Christopher and Augustine prove that the codex was intended for the writer's home convent, the Augustinian canonry of Steterburg, which had been reformed in 1452 according to the Windesheim customs. — On March 18, 1572, it was transferred with the other Steterburg codices to the court library in Wolfenbüttel.


The codex consists of the leaves of at least three palimpsested manuscripts. One of these is a breviary with the office of St. Ansver, which points to an origin in the dioceses of Lübeck, Ratzeburg, Schleswig, or Schwerin

details.value:
Ornate sentence and initial capital letters. 3 initials.
Decorated sentence and initial capitals: Some sentences with rubricated sentence capitals, which in the final arrangement or as letter replacements have feather-like curved leaves (profile leaves, cf. 53v), dot decorations (cf. 67v), mythical creature heads (cf. 73r) and buds (cf. 33v).

Initials: At the beginnings of three books, cleft-ribbed initials with cross- or flower-decorated clasps (1v lib. I, 43v lib. 3, 77v lib. 4). In the inner fields, spiral tendrils run in a dynamic pattern, arranged axially symmetrically as a herbaceous plant on 1v. The terminal decoration consists of bulbous leaves, palmette leaves, and profiled palmette leaves with veining/hatching. The tendril/bud variant with the palmette integrated into the flow and the backward-curving bud at the end (1v) is particularly striking. Large bud primordia are present in the tendril forks. A large, winged dragon with a circularly decorated body and a twisted palmette tail serves as a tail substitute on 1v. 5.4–8.0 cm.

details.value:
A split-border initial. Five Lombard silhouettes. Two sketches.
Initial and silhouette Lombards: At the beginning of Gilbertus Crispinus, a cleft initial with single and five-nailed clasps (81v; 3.6 cm). From one clasp arises a palmette shoot filling the central field, another as the initial stem end. The ends contain seeded palmettes and buds. The leaf backs are hatched. At other highlighted text beginnings, Lombards with simple stem-accompanying silhouette decoration (1r, 10v, 58r, 59v, 60r; 2.0–3.9 cm). The Lombard on 10v is indicated in the stem as a cleft initial.

Sketches: On 10r in the upper right corner, a hastily drawn head (en face) with a hood-like headdress (by a later hand; 5.5 cm). On an inlaid strip of parchment, a pen drawing of a hand chained around the neck (contemporaneous hand; 3.6 cm).

Colors: The initial letter is drawn in red, the initial stem columns are filled in green. The tendril in the center is green, the initial stem end is red. The Lombardic strokes are red and green with silhouette decoration in the contrasting color.

value.title: Wolfenbüttel, Herzog August Bibliothek, Cod. Guelf. 905 Helmst.
Lamspringe, Benedictine, Lamspringe, Lower Saxony, Germany,-1138

details.value: The vertical letter stems are decorated with generously lobed, only slightly veined leaf appliqués and show gold pollen against a red background as split filling. The terminal strokes are trefoils or half-palmettes with barely segmented edges and no veins. The initials are surrounded by broad green borders with red outlines, which also enclose the terminal strokes of the letters. The spandrels between the frame and the initial, as well as part of the letter background, are colored blue, while the figures depicted in the figural initials are set against a gold ground. Despite general similarities with the figural initials of the Hamersleben Psalter (Cod. Guelf. 1075 Helmst.), the details of the initial design show that, contrary to the prevailing scholarly opinion (e.g., Wolter-von dem Knesebeck, Lamspringe , 474f.), the Hamersleben Psalter probably did not serve as a direct model. However, there is no doubt that the illuminator of Cod. Guelf. 905 Helmst. was familiar with the iconographic program of the Hamersleben Psalter and was inspired by it; see, in more detail, the forthcoming catalogue of illuminated manuscripts, HAB 1 . Specifically included are: 27r historicized initial D for Psalm 26 over 8 lines (approx. 6.8 x 6 cm): Christ, recognizable by the cruciform halo, in a blue tunic heightened with white and a red pallium, heals a young man clothed in a yellowish-brown garment. This serves as a word illustration for Psalm 26:1 ( Dominus illuminatio mea et salus mea).The scene depicted probably represents the healing of the man born blind at the Pool of Siloam (John 9:1–41), during which Christ proclaims himself the Light of the World (John 9:5). Since the scrolls held by both figures in their left hands are blank, a definitive identification is not possible. 41r Historicized initial D to Psalm 38 over 8 lines (approx. 6.8 x 65 cm): A youthful, golden-nimbed saint in a frontal half-figure, wearing a blue tunic heightened with white and a red pallium, his right hand half-raised in a gesture of speech, holding a book with red fittings in his left. A more precise identification is not possible based on the attributes; it is evidently a word illustration for Psalm 38:2 ( Dixi custodiam vias meas ut non delinquam in lingua mea posui ori meo custodiam ). 53v Historicized initial Q to Psalm 51 over 7 lines (6 x 6.5 cm): The youthful Christ (half-figure) with a cruciform halo, yellowish-brown tunic, and red pallium addresses Satan in a speech-like gesture. Satan is depicted as a wolf-like animal with grayish-brown fur, pointing to three stones represented as round spheres, which Christ is to transform into bread. Both figures hold blank scrolls, so that the exact source of the scene of the first temptation (Matthew 4:3–4 or Luke 4:3–4) can no longer be determined. The choice of representation is probably motivated by Psalm 51:3 ( Quid gloriaris in malitia qui potens in iniquitate ). 54r Historicized initial D to Psalm 52 over 5 lines (approx. 4.5 x 5.5 cm): Bust of a gold-crowned king with a green undergarment and a red cloak fastened at the right shoulder with a clasp, his right hand half-raised in a speaking gesture, holding a book with red fittings in his left. It is not entirely clear how the depiction relates to the traditional insipiens shown (Psalm 52:1). 68r Figurative initial S to Psalm 68 over 9 lines (approx. 7.5 x 6 cm): Design differs from the historicized initials; the frame consists of a red (top), green (right), brown (bottom), and blue (left) strip. Against a gold background stands a two-legged, red-and-blue winged dragon (lindworm), whose coiled body, colored in three stripes of green, pink, and brown, forms the letter. 85v Initial E to Psalm 80 over 7 lines (approx. 5.5 x 5.5 cm): In a slightly right-turned half-figure, a golden-nimbed, crowned king (David?) with a green undergarment and a red cloak fastened at the right shoulder with a clasp, holding a golden orb in his right hand and a golden scepter with a blue lily-like crown in his left. 102r Initial CPsalm 97, over 7 lines (approx. 5.8 x 5 cm): Half-figure of a haloed woman with long, flowing hair, a crown-like diadem, and a blue undergarment and red outer garment, holding both hands half-raised in an orant gesture. 104r Initial D , for Psalm 101, over 8 lines (approx. 6.5 x 7 cm): Ascension of Christ according to the type of the vanishing Christ, who has risen so far from the centrally located altar-like stone that only his legs and the lower part of his blue tunic with white highlights and his red pallium are visible. The scene is observed by four figures depicted as busts, with golden halos: above, two blue-clad angels holding empty scrolls; below, on the left, Mary in red; and below, on the right, the youthful beloved disciple John. The chosen scene corresponds thematically to Psalms 101:17 and 101:20. For the depiction, see A. Worm , Steine ​​und Fußspuren Christi auf dem Ölberg. Zu zwei ungewöhnlichen Motiven bei Darstellungen der Himmelfahrt Christi, in: Zeitschrift für Kunstgeschichte 66 (2003), 297–320, here 303f. with fig. 9. 118r Initial D to Psalm 109 over 6 lines (approx. 5 x 6 cm): A youthful, red-robed, tonsured cleric in frontal half-length, holding a green palm frond in his right hand and an olive-green bound book in his left. The depiction with the martyr's attribute of the palm frond could be interpreted as a word illustration for Psalm 109:2 ( virgam virtutis emittet dominus ex Zion ). At the beginning of each psalm (59r is the initial for Psalm 58, cut out) and at the beginning of each month in the calendar (abbreviated KŁ ), red-outlined gold initials feature stem-accompanying, sometimes deviating from the outline, vegetal and geometric silhouette ornaments in a lively, varied palette of green, red, and blue; in the calendar, only the latter is used. The silhouettes, mostly lobed in simple teardrop or bud shapes, transition into large, curved palmettes. The inner fields contain vegetal (plants, leaves) and geometric elements (medallions, etc.). Some letter bodies are partially or completely replaced by dragon-like mythical creatures or their heads, which spew out silhouette ornaments or initial stems. Details of the fleuronnée and silhouette design can already be found in the older products of the Lamspringe scriptorium, which belong to the so-called "Scriptrix" group; cf. Cod. Guelf. 723 Helmst. The text is consistently rubricated and features alternating red and blue uncial capitals.

It was completed and written out by Sister Elisabeth Eychelberger in the year 1483 after the birth of Christ, during the time of the honorable mother and devout lady, Abbess Magdalena Kastner.

A collection of manuscripts, written primarily on paper, which can be localized to Bamberg. The first part of the manuscript contains a German mirror of salvation. Erasmus Sternhals is identified as its writer in a colophon. The work was probably made for the Bamberg canon Georg von Löwenstein. This is indicated by the depiction of a kneeling canon and several coats of arms on f.56r. The German-language biography of the Holy Bishop Otto, which is bound in afterwards, also refers to Bamberg. It was written down by two Bamberg Poor Clares and completed in 1483. The third work in the collection is a life of Saint Catherine, dated 1488 and also written by a woman.

records.rec_Title: Admont Abbey, Benedictine, Admont, Austria, 1074

details.value: Abbot Wolfhold founded a convent for the education of girls of noble families; Gottfried of Venningen educated thirteen monks later chosen abbots of other monasteries. Abbot Henry VII (1275-97) began restoration work on the community, Engelbert (1297-1331)completed the restoration.

St. Hemma, Countess of Friesach and Zeltschach, founded community after entering convent at Gurk, leaving lands for the building of a monastery near the salt works of Hall. Foundation, however, was not begun until 1072, more than a quarter of a century after the Saint's death. Abbey church was consecrated by Gebhard von Helfenstein, Archbishop of Salzburg, in honour of St. Blasius in 1074. Gebhard also brought twelve monks from Salzburg to start community. In the following century, a school and community of women emerged from a less formal gathering of religious women around the parish church of S Amandus.
The associated nunnery ceased to exist during the Reformation.

records.rec_Title:
Petersfrauen, Benedictine, Salzburg, Austria, 1113-
1583

details.value: Monastery of St Peter in Salzburg
(Their monastic brethren were known as the Petersherren.)

While knitting and needlework were also important activities, the Petersfrauen were especially known for their writing and illustration of Psalters and other liturgical manuscripts. The sisters also ran a school for young women, according to 15th century documentation (Schellhorn, Die Petersfrauen, 147).

- Ursula Satzenhofer, in the second half of the 15th century; translated the treatise “De passione Christi” of Silvester von Rebdorf (now found as Salzburg, St Peter, cod. B VIII 27). She came from the Regensburg convent of Niedermünster to join the Petersfrauen and professed on 9 August 1469. (2VL 8 col. 587).
- Wolfgang Walcher, the Petersfrauen confessor, translated a number of texts for the women in his care. Born in 1460 in Kösching bei Ingolstadt, Walcher had entered St Peter in Salzburg in 1479; became confessor to the Petersfrauen ca. 1490; and died 18 June 1518. (2VL 10, cols. 603-606 and Wolfgang Walchers Magdalenenlobgesang, here p. 245.)
- In winter 1511/1512 and again in 1523, Johann von Staupitz preached to the Petersfrauen. Modern editions of these sermons are available: Johann von Staupitz, Salzburger Predigten 1512 : eine textkritische Edition : philosophische Dissertation angenommen von der Neuphilologischen Fakultät der Universität Tübingen am 12. Juli 1984; Johann von Staupitz, Salzburger Predigten 1520, A mystic’s passion : the spirituality of Johannes von Staupitz in his 1520 Lenten sermons.
- Hans Wildsgeferd, a canon of Augsburg Cathedral (d. 1470) had arranged for books to be copied as a gift for "the religious sisters, prioress, and convent of the church of Saint Peter at Salzburg, so that they would pray to God for him." See The Life and Work of Clara Hätzlerin p. 4.


The women of the Petersfrauen were renowned scribes, creating documents for St. Peter’s use and accepting commissions from neighboring religious communities. The Psalters, breviaries, meditation books, prayer books and other manuscripts that they produced were often decorated with miniatures. The Petersfrauen Gradual (Salzburg, Stift St. Peter, a IX.11) from ca. 1190-1200 is available in facsimile. The lost psalter, prepared for Abbot Otto II Chalchosperger, was cited in the Registrum Ottonis f. 22v; he received the psalter from the Petersfrauen in 1404.

Fifteenth-century manuscripts copied by convent scribes include:
• Salzburg, Erzabtei St. Peter, cod. a II 7, a copy of the Passionstraktat of Johannes von Indersdorf and of Grunde aller Bosheit of Tauler, copied by Anna Ammanin and Erentrudis Schöttlin.
• Salzburg, Erzabtei St Peter, cod. a II 17, Johannes dem Taufer, copied by Erentrudis Schöttlin.
• Salzburg, Erzabtei St Peter, cod. a III 7, copied by Regina Mundtenheimerin.
• Salzburg, Erzabtei St Peter, cod. a III 21, a 1448 copy of Petrus de Alliaco’s Geistliche Lieder, copied by Margarethe Hohenwarterin.
• Salzburg, Erzabtei St Peter, cod. a III 28, texts of Hieronymus Posser copied by Katharina Pschachlin.
• Salzburg, Erzabtei St Peter, cod. a IV 22, containing a copy of Thomas Peuntner’s Messerklarungen copied by Erentrudis Schöttlin and a meditation on the mass in prayer form copied by Katharina Pscachlin.
• Salzburg, Erzabtei St Peter, cod. a VI 13, a copy of the Vocabularius ex quo and of Donatus copied by Katharina Pschachlin.
• Salzburg, Erzabtei St. Peter, cod. a VII 35, a miscellany containing Thomas a Kempis, Spruch from Vitas Patrum Albertus Magnus, sermons, and so on, dated 1455 and copied by Anna Ammanin.
• Salzburg, Erzabtei St Peter, cod. b I 1, copied by Barbara (Katharina) Püchlerin.
• Salzburg, Erzabtei St Peter, cod. b I 15, copied by Magdalena Halbergerin.
• Salzburg, Erzabtei St. Peter, cod. b I 24, a Lectionary which includes a prayer copied by Anna Ammanin.
• Salzburg, Erzabtei St Peter, cod. b II 10, a volume of mystic/ascetic texts copied by Eufemia Reitterin.
• Salzburg, Erzabtei St Peter, cod. b II 11, copied in 1523 by Dorothea Meixner.
• Salzburg, Erzabtei St Peter, cod. b III 8 a second volume of mystic/ascetic texts copied by Eufemia Reitterin.
• Salzburg, Erzabtei St Peter, cod. b V 8, copied in 1520 by Dorothea Meixner.
• Salzburg, Erzabtei St. Peter, cod. b V 40, a volume dated 1471 containing works by Tauler, Eckhart, Indersdorf, and Seuse, copied by Anna Ammanin.
• Salzburg, Erzabtei St. Peter, cod. b VI 12, works of Heinrich von Langenstein, copied by Anna Ammanin.
• Salzburg, Erzabtei St Peter, cod. b VIII 27, Silvester von Rebdorf’s Passionsbetrachtungen, etc., copied by Erentrudis Schöttlin.
• Salzburg Nonnberg cod. 23 D +29, Ps.-Augustinus, including the Manuale de verbo dei of Wolfgang Walcher, copied by Barbara (Katharina) Püchlerin and Dorothea Meixner.

The convent of Lichtenthal had an extensive library (see Manuscript sources). It possessed several Psalters, Breviaries, Graduals, Sermons, and lives of the saints. Several works were produced by a "Margaretha dicta Regula" during the course of the fifteenth century, including a Diurnal, Breviary, Solioquies of Bonaventura, Book of holy maids and women, Evangeliar., Leben der Altväter, Paradisus anime, The spiritual rosegarden, and Legend aurea.

records.rec_Title: Lamspringe, Benedictine, Lamspringe, Lower Saxony, Germany,-1138

details.value: Lamspringe; sanctus Adrianus monasterium (873); ecclesia sancti Adriani lamesprinche (1149); ecclesia in Lamesprigge (1169); monasterium beatorum Adriani et Dyonisii martirum in Lammespringhe (1338)

The Herzog-August Bibliothek in Wolfenbüttel possesses 18 manuscript volumes, which belonged to the library of the convent. These are primarily theological and spiritual works, written from the tenth to the sixteenth century. Other documents are located in the HauptStaatsarchiv in Hannover.

A book from the convent (preserved in the Herzog-August-Bibliothek) mentions the nun Ermengarde (c. 1178/1205) as the scribe and as the painter of a miniature of S. Augustine. It is thus likely that the convent did possess a scriptorium (Römer, 370). There are 18 extant books from the convent, 12 stem from the twelfth century. Of the twelve, there are four works of Augustine, two of Gregory the Great, two from Venerable Bede, and one each by Hieronymus, Clemens, John Chrysostomos, and Hugo of S. Victor. The Herzog-August Bibliothek in Wolfenbüttel possesses 18 manuscript volumes, which belonged to the library of the convent. These are primarily theological and spiritual works, written from the tenth to the sixteenth century. Other documents are located in the HauptStaatsarchiv in Hannover.

A book from the convent (preserved in the Herzog-August-Bibliothek) mentions the nun Ermengarde (c. 1178/1205) as the scribe and as the painter of a miniature of S. Augustine. It is thus likely that the convent did possess a scriptorium (Römer, 370). There are 18 extant books from the convent, 12 stem from the twelfth century. Of the twelve, there are four works of Augustine, two of Gregory the Great, two from Venerable Bede, and one each by Hieronymus, Clemens, John Chrysostomos, and Hugo of S. Victor. Römer ascribes these works to the influence of provost Gerhard (1178-1205) (Römer, 335).

Sometimes also language mixing, e.g. (309 v -320 r ) Easter song, Salve centies millesies milies gloriosissima … festa dies paschalis … with longer Low German parts.

See the entry on fol. 1r:
“This book was commissioned to be written by the venerable in God, Lady Anna Gurr, abbess of the venerable convent at Neuburg, and it was completed on the feast of St Quirinus the holy martyr in the year of the Lord 1501, in the first year [of her abbacy].”

Anna Gurr († 1517) was abbess of the Benedictine convent of Neuburg an der Donau until 1509; see P. Lindner, Monasticon episcopatus Augustani antiqui, Bregenz 1913, p. 132 no. 180.
After the dissolution of their convent in 1554, the Neuburg nuns partly moved to Kühbach; thus the ownership note on fol. 1r is probably to be dated after 1554:
“This book belongs to Anna Rinckhamerin, nun of the convent at Kühbach.”

The university library in Augsburg preserves two Breviaries from 1484 and 1486 respectively, owned by Adelheid Sparneck, #Oet.-Wall. II. 1.4o37/ Oett.-Wall. II. 1. 4o39/ and a life of S. Katherine of Alexandria from 1465/66, written by Martha Peurlin, Oett.-Wall. III. 1. 2o12/ a martyrology from the fifteenth century, Oett.-Wall. III. 1. 2o20/ a Vitas patrum from the fifteenth century, Oett.-Wall. III. 1. 2o25/ and Spiritual meditations, 1435, written by Joh. Liephart and owned by Martha Geringin, Oett.-Wall. III. 1. 4o5. The Staatsbibliothek in Bamberg preserves a Processionale, 1497, # HV Msc. 348 (Nro. 147) as well as # Bibl. 73, Williramus, In Cant. cant. 1523, written by A. Brunner, and # Lit. 71, 72, 92, 93, 105, 106, 107, 108, 109, 109d, 130, a Processionale, 1499, and # Theol. 65, Buch von der Gemahelschaft Christis, fifteenth century. The Landesbibliothek in Karlsruhe preserves several manuscripts from the community: # St. Georgen Pap. 8a/ St. Georgen Pap. 8b/ St. Peter Perg. 31a, Ritale, fifteenth century/ St. Peter Perg. 38, Berviary, c. 1500/ St. Peter Perg., 39/ St. peter Perg, 53a/ St. Peter Perg. 61/ St. Peter Perg. 64/ St. Peter Perg. 65/ St Peter Perg. 106/ and UH 11. Manuscript # Clm 28309 in the Staatsbibliothek in Munich may also come from this community. A Rituale from the fifteenth century is held in the German national museum in Nürnberg. In The Free Library in Philadelphia, # Lewis Eur. 161 (Phill. 1146), beginning "Super decr." from 1450 may also come from this community.

Vinnenberg cloister, Benedictine, Warendorf, Germany,-1465
1810

details.value:
https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kloster_Vinnenberg
The first abbess mentioned in the chronicle was a certain Angela. She is said to have governed her monastery with "all reverence and spiritual zeal" and died in 1301. From this time onward, a continuous series of 28 abbesses is recorded in the chronicle.
Until the mid-15th century, the monastery was a Cistercian nunnery and subordinate to Marienfeld Abbey in Marienfeld . In the 15th century, the monastery experienced internal and external decline due to its integration into the economic and social structures of the time. Some of the nuns had become secularized, and a few possessed private property. In 1465, at the initiative of Bishop Johann of Münster and Abbot Heinrich von Kleve of Liesborn [ 8 ] , Abbess Ursula Swaneken succeeded in transforming the convent into a Benedictine abbey as part of a renewal of monastic life . From 1468 onward, it belonged to the Bursfeld Congregation and was placed under the authority of Liesborn Abbey .

Prayer book:
 • 57r–71r: Passion prayers beginning “Protect me at all times and especially at my last departure…” including (on 59r) a list of saints predominantly of Dominican origin.
70r: Morning prayer addressed to Eternal Wisdom: “O most beautiful, most radiant, eternal Wisdom…”

 • 88r–100v: Prayer by St. Bernard when Jesus descended to him from the Cross: “Hail, Jesus, the salvation of the world…”
 • 101r: Blank.
 • 101v: Rubric for the Rosary of Christ, incomplete.
 • 142r–153v: Exhortation for the contemplation of the sovereignty of God, German, ,

details.value:
Rosalie Green, Michael Evans, Christine Bischoff, and Michael Curschmann(ed.) (1979) The Hortus Deliciarum of Herrad of Hohenbourg (Landsberg, 1176-96): A Reconstruction. Warburg Institute/E.J. Brill
Fiona J. Griffiths (2007) The Garden of Delights: Reform and Renaissance for Women in the Twelfth Century. Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press.

The Hortus deliciarum is a Christian encyclopedic manuscript, produced between 1159 and 1175 by Herrade of Landsberg (also known as Herrade of Hohenbourg) and the nuns of the convent of Hohenbourg Abbey (Mount Sainte Odile). The original manuscript was destroyed in the fire at the Strasbourg Library on 24 August 1870.

It is the earliest known encyclopedia produced by a woman. Written in Latin, the work summarizes both theological and secular knowledge of its time.

The original manuscript, which had been transferred to the Strasbourg Library during the French Revolution, was destroyed in the 1870 fire during the Franco-Prussian War. The miniatures are known to us through partial copies made by Christian Moritz Engelhardt and by Auguste de Bastard d'Estang. In most cases, the original captions were ignored during the copying process (see the section “Reconstruction of the original”).

Mostly watermarks already known from other St Catherine manuscripts: 	•	Characteristic ox-head types in various forms, including: 	•	Ox-head with eyes and nostrils, with staff and “Z” (e.g. fol. 3), as in Codd. sang. 363 and 1916 (here: right eye placed higher, right ear hanging downward, right cheek indented). 	•	Mitre-like mark (fol. 4), as in Codd. sang. 363, 406, 1916. 	•	Small crown (from fol. 19 onward), as in Cod. sang. 1066. 	•	Female head (from fol. 106 onward), as in the Urbar register booklet. Watermarks not previously attested in other St Catherine manuscripts: 	•	Small, somewhat misshapen ox-head (fols. 66–69), visible especially on fol. 67, somewhat similar to Piccard II/2 (1966), VII, no. 226 (Basel, Strasbourg 1489), though that model has a staff with star as subsidiary mark (possibly here not visible?); not recorded in Briquet. 	•	Chalice (fol. 135; clearly visible fols. 155 and 167), very similar to Briquet no. 4546 (Sion 1490; Lucerne 1492; Freiburg im Breisgau 1494). 	•	Toward the end: large crown (lower part visible fol. 175; upper part fol. 180). Watermarks allow only approximate chronological placement (1480s), not precise dating.

The designation “Schwesternbuch” is misleading.

It does not correspond to what scholarship usually calls a “Sisters’ Book,” namely:

“a seemingly chronicle-like compilation of numerous short vitae of deceased sisters of a particular convent, produced by members of the subsequent generation of sisters” (Ringler, 1980, p. 4).

The St Gall Schwesternbuch shares with that genre:
	•	a chronicle-like character (Part I)
	•	gradual textual expansion
	•	didactic and edifying function (Part II)

However, it should not, as has unfortunately happened in older scholarship, be misinterpreted—especially in its second part—as a document presenting exemplary traditions of spiritual life at St Katharina, St Gall.

That literary type arose in the first half of the 14th century as a female counterpart to the Vitas fratrum (see Meyer, Katharinental, 1995, p. 23).

details.value: Two Merovingian saints from Hesbaye, who were successively abbesses of Aldeneik on the Meuse. According to their Vita, the two sisters had received a careful education: they had learned to read, to sing, to paint, and to write—activities which, their biographer notes, even strong men would have found arduous. They later settled in the family monastery, where they devoted themselves, among other things, to passementerie work to embellish ritual garments. They also copied, again according to their biographer, the Gospels, a psalter, and other sacred writings.

details.value: large ox head with staff and diagonal bar, without eyes or nostrils, with very small ears; the line continues upward past the ears. It is quite similar to Gerhard Piccard, Wasserzeichen II (1966), no. 253, though that example is dated later (1504–1506, Augsburg). At least two variants of the motif appear in this manuscript (see fols. 116–117, where the ears and skull differ).

details.value:
The original binding was replaced in the Benedictine monastery of Clus, after the codex was supplemented there around 1510, by a late Gothic wooden-board binding with an undyed sheepskin cover (flesh side outward).
This is remarkable insofar as the Augustinian canonesses of Marienberg belonged not only to a different monastic observance, but also to a different reform association—the Windesheim Congregation of the Augustinian Canons—and were in fact supervised and visited by the prior of the neighboring Augustinian canons’ house of Hamersleben, who was also responsible for the standardization of liturgical books according to Windesheim requirements, as Cod. Guelf. 501 Helmst. shows. The correction work of the Benedictines of Clus on this codex is a striking example of collaboration among reformed religious across the boundaries of their own association.

records.rec_Title: Nuremberg, Stadtbibliothek, Cent. VI 53
Überlingen, Leopold-Sophien-Bibliothek, Ms. 22

details.value:
On the flyleaf fol. I there is a watermark that cannot otherwise be detected in the manuscript and probably comes from the bookbinder’s stock: ox head with staff and diagonal bar (|| 60 mm), very similar, if not identical, to Ravensburg paper Piccard Ox Head V 353 (southwestern Germany [including Constance], 1498–1506) and Briquet 15258 (Schaffhausen 1506).

Codicological units A and B:
(1) Double tower with three battlements and one window per tower, without countermark, clearly visible on fol. 2 and 202–204, identical with Piccard, Tower IV 32, and Piccard online no. 101207 (Biberach, Sigmaringen 1504, 1505).
(2) Ox head (|| 57 mm) with single-contour staff and cross, eyes and nostrils, very similar, if not identical, to Piccard Ox Head VII 83 (southwestern Germany [including Constance and St. Gallen], 1501–1510).

Codicological units C and D: letter P, broken, double-contoured, with countermark, above it a four-leaf clover (only fragmentary) on fol. 278, within a bifolium inserted into the eighth quire [fol. 278–279, different paper, medium-strong ribbing], identical with Piccard Letter P IX 676, fragment (Constance 1505). The same watermark is also found in the manuscripts Überlingen, Leopold-Sophien-Bibliothek, Mss. 1 (Regina Sattler) and 16 (1504, Cordula von Schönau), as well as Freiburg im Breisgau, Archiepiscopal Archive, Hss. 27 (1506/1507, Regina Sattler and Cordula von Schönau) and 28 (Regina Sattler and Cordula von Schönau).

For the production process of Ms. 22 (= Ü), Simone Mengis assumes that Cordula von Schönau, after completing the first two codicological units A and B in Constance, sent the blank fascicles to St. Gallen, where Regina Sattler wrote units C and D. However, two passages in the codices Freiburg im Breisgau, Archiepiscopal Archive, Hs. 28, and Überlingen, Leopold-Sophien-Bibliothek, Ms. 5, likewise written by the two convent sisters, where the hands of the two scribes change in the middle of a sentence, show that Cordula von Schönau and Regina Sattler were active, at least temporarily, in the same place. Even though Regina Sattler’s stay in the Zoffingen convent is not documented by charters, this place, according to the dates 1504 and 1506/1507, the identity of the paper with that of units C and D of Ü, and the bindings of several manuscripts written individually or jointly by the two Dominican nuns, cannot have been the Dominican convent in St. Gallen, but only the Dominican convent of Zoffingen in Constance, where Cordula von Schönau is demonstrably present from 1497 onward.

value.title: Heidelberg, Universitätsbibliothek, Pal. germ. 807; Part 1: f. 1–63

details.value:
363 prescriptions for various illnesses, in no particular order. Recipe contributors, people on whom the remedies were tested, and informants are not named.

1. Fols. 1v–2v: 16 prescriptions concerning which herbs are used or applied.
2. Fol. 3v: Note: all the entries written in this book are crossed out, not because they are wrong or objectionable, but because they are all written elsewhere in another book. The lines are marked so that what is written here should not be written again. Marginal note: “Note.”
3. Fols. 4r–7v: 28 recipes for diseases of the mouth, throat, and teeth.
4. Fols. 8r–10v: 17 plague recipes. Heading: “For the pestilence.”
5. Fols. 11v–12v: 10 recipes for erysipelas / “rose.”
6. Fols. 13r–15v: 24 recipes for various illnesses: fever, dysentery or “red belly,” abdominal pain, poisoning.
7. Fols. 16r/v: 9 recipes for coughs and chest ailments.
8. Fols. 17r–18v: 16 recipes for diseases of the body and abdomen.
9. Fols. 18v–23r: 29 recipes for various illnesses: headache, dizziness, hallucinations, stomach problems, liver problems, abscesses, blood purification, stroke.
10. Fols. 24r–29v: 40 recipes for women’s illnesses.
11. Fols. 30r–31v: 15 recipes for jaundice and dropsy.
12. Fols. 32r–34r: 19 recipes for various illnesses: stone, stroke, epilepsy, fever, and other conditions.
13. Fols. 34v–35r: 11 recipes for the ears.
14. Fol. 35v: 6 recipes for the eyes.
15. Fols. 36r/v: 6 recipes against wounds.
16. Fols. 37r–38r: 15 recipes against various illnesses, including worms in the stomach, colic, rage, and heart pain.
17. Fols. 38r–39v: 17 recipes for teeth and gums.
18. Fols. 39v–44v: 36 recipes for various diseases, including cancer or boils, fistulas, scabies, spots, etc.
19. Fols. 45v–47v: 12 recipes for wounds.
20. Fols. 48r–53r: 35 recipes for various illnesses and cosmetics.
21. Fols. 54r–56v: 11 recipes for edema, sores, ruptures, and scabies.
22. Fols. 57v–58r: Sage tract, not in Hlawitschka. Heading: “How one should make the water of virtues, this drink of youth…”
23. Fols. 58r–62r: 10 recipes for various illnesses, especially stomach, head, and wounds.
24. Fols. 62v–63r: Index. Alphabetical list of indications in Latin and German, referring to fols. 4–61, equivalent to modern fols. 1–58.
25. Fol. 63r: At the upper margin, beginning of a recipe: “For the swelling under the…” It breaks off.

Fols. 3r, 11r, 23v, 45r, 53v, 55v, 57r, 58v, and 63v are blank.

records.rec_Title: Christina Ebner, Female

details.value: Christina Ebner (1277–1356) was a German mystic at the Dominican convent of Engelthal, who wrote, in the vernacular, her experiences of grace and divine revelations (Leben und Offenbarungen) and the Engelthal sister book. In the fourteenth century, Engelthal was a wealthy, noble convent with a rich culture of mystical spirituality and literary activity. Ebner’s mystical revelations survive in two separate texts that record her experiences of God’s grace and presence, dialogues with Christ, temptation by the devil, and Ebner’s ascetic and spiritual practices, while the sister book chronicles the history of Engelthal and the mystical experiences of its deceased sisters, patrons, and chaplains.

details.value: This manuscript contains The Divine Prophecies of the Ten Sibills, written and illuminated by Jane Segar, sister of the Elizabethan herald and officer of arms Sir William Segar (b. c. 1554, d. 1633) and the courtier and painter Francis Segar (b. 1563, d. 1615). Jane presented the volume to Elizabeth I (r. 1558-1603) in 1589, probably as a New Year's gift, and prefaced the work with a prose dedication to the Queen.

details.value: Hamburger, Jeffrey F. « Magdalena Kremer, scribe and painter of the choir and chapter books of de Dominican convent of St Johannes-Baptista in Kirchheim unter Teck ». In Glosses Christopher de Hamel. 2010: "According to the document preserved by sattler, among the nuns who came to kirchheim was ‘ein swester . . . die konde wol textur schriben, und och malen’.11 the author of the document—most likely, given the numerous references to scribal activity, the ‘texturschriberin’ herself—instructed a pair of nuns in calligraphy and illumination at the Dominican convent at Pforzheim during the two days the sisters from silo sojourned there while en route to kirchheim. Later in the same account, this nun is named (or names herself) as ‘Magdalena kremerin, die kam von stroßburg gan syl’ (who came to silo from strasbourg). this is the same Magdalena kremer who wrote the convent’s chronicle and who became prioress of the community in 1495 and served until 1501/1502."

Sessinghaus, Scholastica

Scholastica was elected abbess of Kloster Vinnenberg around July 19, 1547, by Bishop Franz von Waldeck, succeeding Hillegund Hoyer. During her term, the monastery church underwent two devastating fires in 1550 and 1568. She compiled a calendar and index for the monastery around 1560. She died sometime before March 26 1572, when Johann von Hoya, Bishop of Münster, appointed her successor Dorothea Peicks. (from himml: https://haf.vhmml.org/person/832310079740)
